articles.title: Who is Mehrdad Akhlaghi, Iran’s new tech-focused defence minister?
articles.body:
Who is Mehrdad Akhlaghi, Iran’s new tech-focused defence minister?
Akhlaghi’s experience centres on ballistic missiles, aerospace technology and defence-industrial production.
Tehran, Iran – Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi has been appointed Iran’s defence minister at a time when the war with the United States is expected to escalate.
The 68-year-old was approved on Sunday by parliament, which has convened online since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran on February 28, to assume leadership of the Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics. In total, 237 lawmakers voted in favour of Akhlaghi’s appointment and 15 against.
Former Defence Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed along with a large number of other senior figures, including Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, on the opening day of the war.
The position was filled temporarily by Majid Ebn-e Reza, who will now become Akhlaghi’s deputy.
Akhlaghi will be responsible for rebuilding and expanding Iran’s military-industrial infrastructure, which has been heavily targeted by the US and Israel.
The new minister’s defence plans were approved earlier by senior military authorities, President Masoud Pezeshkian and parliament’s Commission on National Security and Foreign Policy.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran will not be the instigator of aggression against any country but will defend the territorial integrity of the country strongly and to the death against any aggression,” Pezeshkian said.
The president said Akhlaghi has more than 42 years of experience in the Defence Ministry and related organisations.
His principal expertise is in ballistic missiles, solid-fuel propulsion, aerospace technology and military-industrial production, according to state media.
Previously, he served as the head of the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, the Aerospace Industries Organization and the Defence Industries Organization. Akhlaghi and these entities are all subject to sanctions by the US. He is also under United Nations sanctions.
He has been associated with developing several missile types and related weapons-development projects over the past decades, according to Tasnim, a newspaper linked with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC),
Akhlaghi reportedly played a role in expanding the major Sejjil and Zolfaghar family of Iranian ballistic missiles as well as precision-guided weapons, such as the Almas missiles and Yasin guided bombs.
He is also said to have expertise in space launchers, research rockets and infrastructure associated with the Imam Khomeini Space Center in Semnan. These have all been critical elements in Iran’s wars against Israel and the US.
This month, Iran’s Defence Ministry spokesman, Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik, told reporters that Akhlaghi’s nomination reflected Iran’s need to increase the quantity and quality of strategic weapons, particularly missiles and drones.
“Offensive arms are being actively improved,” the spokesman said.
The US has repeatedly claimed that it has destroyed most of Iran’s military-industrial capacities, but Tehran has maintained it continues to have considerable offensive and defensive capabilities outside the reach of US and Israeli bombs. These weapons have been upgraded based on Iran’s new war experience, it has insisted.
Akhlaghi told members of parliament this month that he had met with senior military commanders, including the commander-in-chief of the IRGC, Brigadier General Ahmad Vahidi, to develop a better understanding of their requirements during and after the war.
His priorities as defence minister would be faster military-industrial development, air defences, incorporation of emerging technologies using government and private sector firms, improvements in armed-forces welfare and development of international military cooperation, according to reports.
In his first comments as defence minister on Sunday, Akhlaghi taunted the administration of US President Donald Trump, which this month threatened to use the “mother of all bombs” on Iran’s nuclear and energy infrastructure.
“We have made preparations and continue our work with ease of mind,” he told reporters. “The US president must think of getting his forces out of our region in one piece. If he drops one bomb, he must see how many of his troops he will have to evacuate horizontally.”

articles.title: Zelenskyy Says Russia Seeking 'Total Blackout' In Ukraine After Latest Onslaught On Energy Facilities
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian strikes overnight targeted power substations in multiple regions, leaving tens of thousands of households without electricity, as Ukrainian and Russian officials reported civilian deaths following overnight drone attacks on October 18.
Zelenskyy said Russia had carried out 76 attacks on Ukraine's energy and oil and gas sectors in the week since US President Donald Trump announced an energy cease-fire. Trump said on October 11 that he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to observe a weeklong pause in attacks on energy infrastructure amid freezing weather in Ukraine.
"Over the past week, Russia launched nearly 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs, and 66 missiles at Ukraine, most of them ballistic missiles," Zelenskyy wrote on social media on October 18.
Accusing Moscow of seeking to plunge Ukraine into a nationwide blackout, Zelenskyy wrote on social media: "Russia is not taking steps toward peace."
Zelenskyy said that power stations were targeted in the Vinnytsya, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskiy, and Odesa regions in the overnight strikes.
Russian attacks killed at least two people and injured several others in Ukraine, Ukrainian officials said.
In the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhya, a 27-year-old woman was killed and two people were injured, including a six-year-old girl, according to the regional military administration.
The attacks damaged two apartment buildings, 18 cars, and an educational institution, the administration said.
In the central city of Poltava, a Russian drone attack killed one woman and injured four other people, the head of the city's military administration, Vitaliy Dyakivnych, said on Telegram. Nine residential buildings were damaged, some by falling drone debris.
In the western Vinnytsia region, Russian drone attacks on critical infrastructure caused power outages, the regional military administration said.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia had launched 180 combat drones during the overnight attacks, of which 152 were intercepted. Impacts were recorded at 20 locations, it said.
Russia Reports Casualties, Infrastructure Damage
In Russia, one person was killed and five injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on St. Petersburg, the city's governor, Aleksandr Beglov, said on October 18.
Fires broke out at the St. Petersburg oil terminal, an oil depot, and industrial warehouses, Beglov said. Twelve apartment buildings were also damaged.
Russian e-commerce company Ozon said a drone struck one of its logistics facilities in St. Petersburg, causing a fire. Employees were evacuated, and no one was injured at the facility, the company said.
The VK Internet company said its data center in the Leningrad region had also been targeted by drones, but its services remained available to users as normal.
A drone struck a cable-stayed bridge forming part of St. Petersburg's Western High-Speed Diameter highway. The extent of the damage was not immediately clear.
The attacks also caused power disruptions in parts of the region. Two transformer substations in Yanino were reportedly disconnected, while operations at St. Petersburg's Pulkovo Airport were disrupted.
Russia's Defense Ministry said air defense units had downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight. The figure could not be independently verified.
Drone attacks also disrupted air travel across Russia. More than 350 flights were delayed or canceled at Moscow's four airports overnight on October 17, as authorities imposed restrictions amid reported Ukrainian drone attacks on the Moscow region.
The figures were based on airport departure and arrival boards reviewed by the independent Russian outlet Meduza.
Sheremetyevo was the worst affected, with 143 flights canceled and 53 delayed. Vnukovo recorded 55 cancellations and 113 delays, while Domodedovo reported 59 delayed flights. Some flights bound for Moscow were diverted to other cities, including St. Petersburg and Nizhny Novgorod.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said Russian air defenses had destroyed 75 drones heading toward the capital. Russia's Defense Ministry said more than 600 drones had been destroyed or intercepted across the country overnight, Interfax reported.
Airports in Penza, Saratov, and Sochi also suspended operations.
Kyiv Says Starshield Connections Still Limited
The latest barrage on Ukraine came as disruptions to the Starshield satellite system, the military-grade version of the Starlink service run by Elon Musk's SpaceX, left Ukraine particularly vulnerable earlier in the week.
On October 17, Kyiv said the speed of Starshield connections across Ukrainian territory remained significantly limited, causing instability in battlefield communications, medium-range strikes, and the operation of interceptor drones.
"The shortage of air defense systems, combined with the lack of confirmation that Starshield's full operational capabilities have been restored, creates additional challenges for Ukraine in protecting critical infrastructure against Russian aerial attacks," Denys Sienik, Ukraine's charge d'affaires to the United States, told RFE/RL.
"With colder weather approaching and winter drawing nearer, we fully understand the deliberate nature of Russia's strategy: to systematically damage Ukraine's energy infrastructure and leave civilians without essential services," he added.
On October 17, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected claims that the United States had deliberately restricted Ukraine’s access to Starlink, the satellite Internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
"No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down Internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it," he told reporters on October 17 as he prepared to depart for Central Asia, calling reports of US involvement "categorically false."
Rubio said his understanding was that Starlink's performance had returned to its previous level. Ukraine had used the commercial service to support drone operations.
He also questioned the Ukrainian president's account of the incident, saying he was "not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about."
Rubio distinguished Starlink from Starshield, a separate defense-oriented satellite system used by the US military.
Ukraine does not currently have access to Starshield, he said, although Kyiv has requested it to conduct deep strikes inside Russia. The question of how the system might be used remains under discussion, Rubio added.
His comments highlighted the limits of Ukraine's access to US-linked military technology as tensions between Washington and Kyiv grow over the administration's approach to Russia.

Trump’s sanctions waiver
‘rewards’ Putin: Zelenskiy
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said yesterday that US President Donald Trump’s decision to block Russian sanctions only “rewards” Russian President Vladimir Putin and warned that Moscow was trying to deprive “millions” of Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter.
Amid a clash with the Ukrainian wartime leader, Trump signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions targeting Russia’s energy revenues. The decision came despite Russia increasing strikes on Ukraine — especially its capital, Kyiv — in the fifth year of its offensive, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
The Lindsey Graham Act — named after the deceased US senator who sponsored the bill — targeted Russia’s energy and defense sectors, as well as Putin and the so-called “shadow fleet” of tankers used by Moscow to circumvent Western sanctions.
Photo: Getty images via AFP
Zelenskiy said the decision came the same day as Russia attacked 15 critical power generation facilities across Ukraine in “one of the largest” attacks on Ukraine’s energy grid.
“It is important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening,” he said on social media. The Lindsey Graham Act, he said, was “supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end,” adding that the act “could have helped enormously — and still can!”
“A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” he said.
The Ukrainian leader said Russia wanted to cause a “blackout” in Ukraine ahead of winter: “Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating.”
He called on allies to keep up pressure on Moscow to “stop this.”
Last winter saw hundreds of thousands in Ukraine consistently without heat and electricity in freezing temperatures. A day after Trump waived the sanctions, causing Europe and Kyiv to worry which side of the war the White House is on, Ukraine said at least two people were killed in Russian airstrikes.
Officials said one person was killed in the southern city of Kherson in an attack that also wounded 22 people, including two children, and that another was killed in the northeastern city of Sumy.
The Kremlin and Putin have not yet reacted to Trump, but several Russian officials celebrated the move as a win.
“The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment,” Kirill Dmitriev, a Putin envoy, said on social media.
Dmitriev said the act would have caused “serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets.”
Trump’s waiver comes after he struck a deal with Putin to ease sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel onto global markets.
He announced the executive order on Friday, shortly after Putin appeared in military uniform and said that Moscow aims to capture the rest of east Ukraine.
Ukraine has been struggling to shoot down Russian missiles and has been left scrambling to boost defenses ahead of winter.
Russia controls large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine and Putin has repeatedly said that Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine by force.
“On the whole I see a positive trend in the operations of the troop groupings,” Putin told army leaders on Friday, dressed in military attire.
“Undoubtedly, one of the main objectives remains the liberation of the Donetsk People’s Republic,” he added, using the Kremlin’s name for the eastern Donetsk region.

articles.title: Ukraine still can't intercept drones due to Starlink issues, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Ukraine still unable to intercept Russian drones due to Starlink restrictions, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine is still unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday, because of speed restrictions imposed on Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink, amid an ongoing row with President Trump.
"Unfortunately, we can't use Starlink or Starshield technology on our territory today to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds," Zelenskyy said in an online group chat with reporters at the EU Summit. "They fly, and we can stop them with aircraft and other air defense, but we don't use Starlink for that, unfortunately. God willing, this will be restored."
Zelenskyy said Kyiv was discussing the issue with U.S. officials, and he was told the restrictions were linked to technical issues. The Ukrainian president added, however, that Starlink appears to be operating at higher speeds on European Union territory.
"Yes, we are in dialogue at the level of the military, the Ministry of Defense and diplomats, in touch with everyone including SpaceX. Nobody there is answering our military or the Ministry of Defense now," Zelenskyy said. "At various levels they say these are technical problems."
"Here (in Ukraine) Starlink works up to a speed of 161 km/h, then shuts off," he continued. "In the EU it works at 180-plus and works constantly. Here it shuts off in the second minute after 161 km/h and stops working. We lose both drones and connectivity."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, when asked about the situation Saturday on the tarmac of Joint Base Andrews, said, "Starshield is a defense product, a military product, and as I said … that is something that we have, the military, United States military, uses. It's not at this moment available to Ukraine, and that's under conversation. It's under discussion right now about how they would want to use it."
Pushed on whether the U.S. government was responsible for the service outage in Ukraine, Rubio responded, "No," and alleged that Ukraine's military has never had access to Starshield, but has only been using Starlink.
"I don't know what Zelenskyy said, I'm not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about, but it wasn't deliberate," Rubio said. "We had nothing to do with that. I don't, the United States, nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it's been restored, it's back to what it was before."
Rubio went on: "Starshield is a contract with the U.S. military, it has nothing to do with Ukraine. I know Ukraine wants access to Starshield, they do not have Starshield now. They've asked for access to it in order to conduct deep strikes inside of Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment. Those are two different products."
Denys Sienik, the chargé d'affaires of Ukraine to the U.S., told CBS News in a statement later Saturday that Ukraine had still not received a response from the Pentagon or SpaceX regarding its inquiries about Starlink or Starshield service, "including confirmation that unlimited speeds have been restored and that Starshield is operating as it did previously."
Sienik said "based on the data currently available to us, we cannot confirm that these capabilities have been fully restored."
Mr. Trump told reporters on Friday he had not limited Ukraine's access to Starlink, adding he didn't believe Musk, SpaceX's CEO, was responsible either.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Mr. Trump said while leaving the White House to travel for a rally in Georgia. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
Musk said Wednesday he isn't responsible for deciding how Starshield is used, writing on X: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia carried out a large attack on Ukraine's energy sector, targeting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities across the country. A day earlier, the president said the current restrictions on Starshield had left people vulnerable to Russian drones, which was "very painful and frustrating"
Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including speed limits that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions.
Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent days, blaming the war between Russia and Ukraine for high global energy prices. The Trump administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel last week in an effort to ease pressure, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.
In a social media post on Saturday, Zelenskyy called the move "unfortunate," adding the act, championed by late Sen. Lindsey Graham, "could have helped enormously." Later, he told journalists he believed the Trump administration will lift more sanctions on Russia.
"Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the 'diesel deal' is just the first step," Zelenskyy told reporters.
"President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end. As talks continue, this Act provides the President with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CBS News on Saturday in response to a question about lifting the sanctions. "Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests."
Mr. Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire" over the weekend. Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed it had agreed to a ceasefire.
In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," urged both sides to make a deal and said the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin.
"I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said.
On Wednesday, Musk had tweeted: "Time for Zelensky to go."

articles.title: Sanctions strangle Iranian economy as IRGC goes on high alert over civil unrest risks - analysis
articles.body:
Senior Israeli defense officials estimate that economic sanctions are choking the Iranian regime, forcing internal security apparatuses onto high alert to preempt widespread civil unrest.
According to assessments, the Iranian street is simmering, and the next boiling point, driven by American leverage, could arrive within months, though public reaction remains unpredictable.
Simultaneously, the regime is pursuing diplomatic and military maneuvers to break its isolation, conveying threats and engaging in provocative actions across the region. Officials note that Tehran deeply fears an American or Israeli surprise strike and is preparing for extreme scenarios.
Following new US sanctions that took effect on September 23 and targeted flights from Iran, many countries suspended Iranian flights.
While China rejected the sanctions and Turkey reduced flight volumes without fully canceling them, Armenia, Russia, Afghanistan, and Pakistan continue to allow Iranian flights following diplomatic outreach. Pressure on Iraq also secured designated flight corridors (excluding Baghdad).
Iran maintaining proxy network, transfers millions of dollars
Concurrently, Tehran works around the clock to maintain its regional proxy network. Reports from Beirut indicate that approximately $200 million was recently transferred to Hezbollah. Iran also continues providing advice, training, production support, and weapons transfers to the Houthis in Yemen, while preserving ties with pro-Iranian Shia militias in Iraq and seeking new anti-Western partnerships. The objective is to ensure proxy alignment in any future conflict.
To establish deterrence against Gulf states and pressure Washington through them, Tehran has issued threats over the past week indicating a capacity for ground invasions into neighboring countries - a scenario Israel warns could dramatically escalate regional turmoil. These threats accompany reports of naval mine incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and damage to maritime vessels.
Iran resumes ballistic missile production, restores damaged weaponry
According to Israeli sources, Iran has resumed ballistic missile production and is working to restore damaged weaponry alongside completing manufacturing processes initiated before Operation Roaring Lion. "The process is slow and constrained by knowledge gaps and production limits, but they are actively moving in that direction," a defense official noted.
Politically, Tehran is attempting to open diplomatic channels to buy time, restrict American operational flexibility, and prevent further strikes on its territory.
In response, Israel conveyed messages to the US, Gulf nations, and regional mediators stressing that any Iranian surprise offensive will trigger an exceptionally severe military response.
Jerusalem clarified that its objectives regarding Iran's nuclear project, missile array, and defense industry infrastructure are not yet complete. Should Iran initiate an attack, Israel may act with greater force than during Operation Lion's Roar, including strikes on national infrastructure previously limited by Washington to shorten conflict duration.
Defense officials emphasize extremely high operational coordination between the IDF and US Central Command (CENTCOM). Sources in daily contact with American counterparts say that US President Donald Trump has placed the military on high alert, keeping the option of strikes open until the last minute.
However, officials assess that an American strike prior to the US midterm elections remains unlikely unless Iran initiates offensive actions or signals imminent regional aggression.
Consequently, the IDF maintains heightened vigilance, closely monitoring developments in Iran, Lebanon, Yemen, Iraq, and the maritime domain against unexpected aggression from Tehran or its proxies.

articles.title: Iran Parliament approves new defence minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi: State media
articles.body:
Iran Parliament approves new defence minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi: State media
- Iran’s parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaghi as defence minister with 237 votes, replacing Aziz Nasirzadeh after his death in a US-Israeli attack.
- State media said Akhlaghi called the post a duty at a “sensitive juncture” and said defence needs clear thinking and readiness for future threats.
- Akhlaghi has 42 years in the defence ministry and has led the Defence Industries Organisation since 2013, but the UN sanctioned him in 2007 over missile or nuclear activity.
AI generated
TEHRAN – Iranian lawmakers on Oct 18 approved Mehrdad Akhlaghi as the country’s new defence minister, replacing his predecessor who was killed on the first day of the war with the United States.
“Members of the Islamic Consultative Assembly (Parliament) today gave a vote of confidence to Mehrdad Akhlaghi, the nominee for minister of defence and armed forces logistics,” state television reported, nearly eight months after the initial US-Israeli strikes that sparked the conflict.
According to the government website, Akhlaghi “was elected to the post with 237 votes in favour”, out of a total of 277 votes cast.
The veteran defence official replaces Aziz Nasirzadeh, who was killed in a US-Israeli attack on a leadership compound on Feb 28, alongside former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and senior military commanders.
“If I receive parliament’s vote of confidence, responsibility for the Ministry of Defence will fall to me at a sensitive juncture,” Akhlaghi said before the vote, according to the ISNA news agency.
“Under such circumstances, defending the country requires an accurate understanding of the environment, an understanding of the logic behind developments, the identification of influential trends, and preparedness to face different possible futures,” he added.
Although he does not hold a military rank, Akhlaghi has worked in the defence ministry for 42 years and has headed the Iranian Defence Industries Organisation, the state’s weapons manufacturer, since 2013.
The United Nations sanctioned Akhlaghi in 2007 over his alleged involvement in nuclear or ballistic missile activities. AFP

articles.title: I’m a Russian Fashion Designer – Vladimir Putin Is Terrified of Me
articles.body:
Less than five years ago, her life could hardly have been more glamorous or safer. Anastasia Vistorobska worked in Paris for two of the world’s best-known fashion houses. Today her life could hardly be more challenging or dangerous: working as a combat medic for Ukraine’s armed forces on the front line of its brutal all-out war with Russia.
Anastasia’s story is all-the-more remarkable because of her nationality – she is Russian, which means she has volunteered to risk her life fighting against her homeland. For more than two-and-a-half years, she has worked as a combat medic, treating her comrades close to the front line, while also seeing countless others die on the battlefield.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It is physically and mentally exhausting work. Typically, Anastasia’s days are full of both good and bad news. She fought back tears as she talked about the recent death of a close comrade. “The constant death is terrible. It builds up and it makes me sad and angry. I have seen 42 comrades go on a mission but only 38 came back,” she reflects.
However, there are rewarding days too. “On one occasion, a wounded soldier passed on a message through a comrade: ‘Thank you for saving my life.’ That was very inspiring. I am fortunate, too, that I have never had anyone die in my arms.”
On Feb. 24, 2022, when Russia began its all-out invasion, Anastasia was sleeping in a beautiful house in rural France, when suddenly friends started messaging her that the war had started. “They all said the same: that Ukraine was under bombardment. My immediate reaction was: ‘this cannot be happening!’”
Olesia Avramenko: ‘Ukrainian Art Preserves What the World Is Gradually Losing’
At that time, Anastasia, then aged 36, had lived in France for 15 years, for the last seven working in the fashion industry for Chanel and Givenchy as an embroidery designer. With friends and relatives in Ukraine, she typically visited the country twice a year. “After the all-out invasion, I wanted to join the Ukrainian army straightaway but I felt helpless. I was conscious that I had a Russian passport and no previous military experiences. I feared that I would be useless and that no one would take me seriously. But I do have an ability to act decisively. I wanted to go and start killing these invaders.”
As she pondered how to get involved, the Russian massacre of some 500 people at Bucha, near Kyiv, in March 2022, was the final straw. “For me, this was the most horrific moment of the whole war,” she said. Anastasia initially wrote a letter to a military committee in Ukraine explaining: “I know I am Russian but I want to go and defend Ukrainian children. Can you please accept me?”
Her offer was rejected but friends advised her to look into the Freedom of Russian Legion, Russians fighting against their homeland. “I looked at their videos and documentaries and I was astounded by the way they thought and spoke. They seemed to be the best of people and, four years on, having met them, I still feel the same.”
Fearing she was too old and too weak, Anastasia first got herself fitter and stronger over six months before going to Texas, in the US, for a two-month military training course. Eventually, she passed a long vetting procedure and was successful in joining the legion. “The process is strict: Every potential recruit’s background is scrutinized down to the smallest detail to completely eliminate any possibility of FSB [Russian security] infiltration,” she said.
It was not until February 2024, on the second anniversary of the full-scale invasion, that she finally arrived in Ukraine and started undergoing four months of training at a secret location. “It was horrible – really, really hard – but at the end of it I could shoot five different weapons and I learned a lot about the battlefield and communications. I also learned medical skills and evacuation techniques.”
At the end of her training, she chose to work as a combat medic and is now head of a tactical evacuation team. Typically, she operates some six miles from the front line. The aim is that an injured soldier is given basic first aid and evacuated by his comrades, so he or she can receive fuller medical attention from combat medics in slightly safer locations.
I asked Anastasia, who is 5 feet 8 inches (173 cm) tall and of slim build, how she felt fighting a war against her homeland. “I prefer to judge people on their actions rather than their passport. People either do good things or bad things and I want to be on the side of right versus wrong. Stealing land, killing civilians, harming children – they are all wrong.” Strangely perhaps, Anastasia considers it more dangerous to be in Kyiv on leave than she does working close to the front line. The capital is hit almost daily by ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
“In the war zone, I am wearing body armor, I am surrounded by comrades, I am always on alert and I trust my commanders to keep me safe. But in Kyiv this summer I was sleeping in my pajamas on the 14th floor of an apartment building when the area was being hit by missiles and drones. That was terrifying.”
Her worst times have come when comrades are being killed or wounded on the front line. “When you hear someone screaming [for help] on the radio that’s probably one of the hardest moments,” she said.
Anastasia, who left Russia aged 23, has signed a three-year contract with the legion. She does not know yet if she will stay in the army longer because she also has a yearning to go back to her artistic roots. Even now, she applies her talents by creating artistic projects, including making art works from the uniforms of dead soldiers and their belongings. It is intended as a memorial to their sacrifice and, in time, she hopes to exhibit her work. Hundreds of Russians are currently fighting for Ukraine and Anastasia admires them all.
“I am soaked in the stories of my comrades, their chivalry and bravery,” she said. “But what upsets me is that after they die in battle and are cremated, no one [from their family] will come and visit their grave. So I hope my work will commemorate their death, their memory. The huge power of war and art often go hand in hand.”
For security reasons, Anastasia prefers not to discuss details of her family. However, she says all her family members, including her mother, now live outside Russia, which is why she is willing to be identified by name, without fear of reprisals in her homeland.
“I am not scared by the reality that I might get killed. I am just proud to have done a little bit to make the situation better for Ukrainians. Putin is scared of the Legion of Russia which means he is scared of me.”
Her hatred of the Russian president has no limits. She says: “He is one of the biggest war criminals in history. He has been compared to Hitler but he is much worse than Hitler. Putin is destroying Russia even more horribly than he is Ukraine. He stole my pride and my joy at being Russian. He has stolen the right of the Russian language to be the beautiful language it once was.”
She hopes that, once the war ends well for Ukraine, she will be able to divide her time between France and Ukraine. Now aged 41 years old, she is engaged to a Russian man who also serves in the legion. Anastasia says Ukrainians have been largely supportive, rather than suspicious, of her and other Russians fighting for their cause, but she added: “If a Ukrainian was to spit in my face, I would not say a word because I would understand the anger. The reality is that Russia owes a huge debt to Ukraine.”

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine exchange overnight strikes, killing 3 and injuring 21
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
Russia and Ukraine exchanged overnight strikes Sunday, killing three people and injuring 21 others, officials on both sides said.
Ukrainian drones targeted oil facilities and an Ozon logistics center in St. Petersburg, as well as Russian social media company VK’s data center in the Leningrad region.
In St. Petersburg, one person was killed and five others were injured, Gov. Alexander Beglov said on Telegram. The city’s oil terminal, Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses caught fire during a “massive” drone attack.
Beglov said 12 apartment buildings and two private homes were damaged, and emergency crews continued to battle the fires.
An Ozon logistics facility was also hit, sparking a fire and prompting staff to evacuate. No injuries were reported at the site, the company said.
Meanwhile, Leningrad Region Gov. Alexander Drozdenko said four people were hospitalized. Drone debris fell on an apartment building in Gatchina, while 55 parked vehicles were damaged in Novosyolye, he said.
An emergency power outage affected 50 apartment buildings, leaving about 20,000 people without electricity, he added.
Russian social media company VKontakte said its data center in the Leningrad region was also targeted but that its services remained available.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones overnight over Russian territory, Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014, and the Black Sea.
Separately, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said 512 drones headed toward the Moscow region overnight, most of which were destroyed by air defenses at a distance from the capital.
Attacks on Ukraine
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, two people were killed and 12 others injured in Russian overnight strikes on residential buildings across the country, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
In a post on US social media company X, Zelenskyy accused Moscow of “deliberately” attacking Ukraine’s energy, oil, and gas sectors 76 times since US President Donald Trump announced an energy truce between Kyiv and Moscow last week.
He said Moscow targeted substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions overnight, leaving “tens of thousands” of families without power.
Zelenskyy added that Russia had attacked Ukraine with nearly 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic, over the past week, stressing that energy facilities were the main targets.
“And America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” he said. “On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting.”
The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces launched overnight strikes on Ukrainian logistics centers, ports, and vessels allegedly used to support Ukraine’s armed forces.
The ministry said a logistics center operated by Ukrainian postal company Nova Poshta in Rivne was hit. It alleged the facility stored and distributed dual-use goods, including components for long- and medium-range drones.
It added that a cargo ship carrying military and dual-use goods was hit at sea about 30 kilometers (19 miles) east of the port of Odesa.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Air Force said its air defenses shot down or suppressed 152 Russian drones during the overnight attack.
Independent verification of the claims remains difficult due to the ongoing war.

articles.title: 'You are the real target': Netanyahu warns Iran may attempt to develop missiles able to reach US
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Iran was developing intercontinental ballistic missiles and pursuing nuclear weapons with the aim of threatening American cities, telling FOX News on Saturday that the US, rather than Israel, was the Iranian regime's ultimate target.
Netanyahu argued that Iran's ambitions extend beyond Israel, warning that the regime intends to target both the US and Europe if it succeeds in destroying Israel. He said Iran's development of long-range missiles and pursuit of a nuclear arsenal were intended to place American cities at the mercy of the regime.
"They understand that if they can destroy Israel, then they can conquer the Middle East, control the waterways of the world... and then proceed to the next target, which is you. That's why they're building intercontinental missiles: to reach the United States," Netanyahu said.
"This is a regime that chants death to Israel, death to America. You are the real target. And I think we are well on our way to achieving this, with President Trump's brilliant leadership, both military and, then, economic blockade."
The prime minister explained that the Iranian regime views the US as "the great Satan" and Israel as the "little Satan," before directing a remark at European countries.
He said he "hoped our European friends are not offended; you are seen as the middle-sized Satan, you are mediocre in so many ways."
"Iran would be a nuclear power as we've never seen in the entire world, because they don't have this careful calculus of cause and benefit. Because they are so fanatic. So you can't win them over, you can't buy them out," he said.
Netanyahu also described the Iranian regime as a "malevolent power" operating alongside what he called the "Three Hs": Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Houthis.
"They are the arms of this toxic octopus. And it's not Iranian people; they are great people," he added.
Eliminating the Iranian threat was the first of three priorities Netanyahu outlined for his next term if reelected in the October 27 Knesset election, alongside expanding the Abraham Accords and establishing Israel as a global leader in artificial intelligence.
"First, we will achieve the complete elimination of the Iranian threat to Israel, to America, and to the entire world," Netanyahu said.
Expanding Abraham Accords as a key objective
"Second thing is to expand the historic Abraham Accords that [US President Donald] Trump and I forged here with four Arab states," Netanyahu continued.
"There are many more that are waiting in this precise moment, because they saw our strength, our power and fortitude. And they want to join us. So let's create an axis of peace and moderation against these barbarians who shoot their own people," he said.
Netanyahu also said he plans to "forge a different future, a different Middle East, and also a different world" if reelected.
Artificial Intelligence to help humankind
Netanyahu's third priority focused on artificial intelligence, and the prime minister said he agreed with Trump on both the dangers the technology poses and its potential benefits for humanity.
"I plan to seize the future with the 'Neverland AI,' the 'super intelligence,' as the president calls it. He is absolutely right; they are dangerous, but their possibilities in health, in agriculture, in transport, and in education," he explained.
"You can personalize AI for every child; they have their own potential, and you can give them the best teachers on the planet. We are doing it today in Israel, and we intend to be the world leaders in that area too. These are all amazing things," he added.
Netanyahu also pointed to Israel's economic performance, which he described as among the strongest in the developed world.
"By the way, the economy, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), is leading all the Western countries, the OCD countries, with the greatest growth. That's after three years of war. I want to push that even further, bring a better future to Israel, to our neighbors, to our great ally the United States."

articles.title: Russia hit Ukraine’s energy 76 times during a US-declared truce—and tens of thousands lost power overnight. Civilians killed and injured
articles.body:
Russia has kept striking Ukraine’s energy sector throughout the week since US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 18 October. From overnight into Sunday, Russian drones and a ballistic missile hit substations, homes, and industrial sites from Odesa to Volyn. They killed civilians and left tens of thousands of families without power.
Russia fights along the front line while hitting cities and the grid behind it with drones, missiles, and glide bombs. Ukraine says Moscow plans up to 1,000 such munitions against 60 key infrastructure sites this winter, and jet-powered drones partly free it to concentrate missiles on fewer targets, the Institute for the Study of War assessed. With Graham Act penalties on hold and US sanctions on Russian diesel suspended, Russia faces no new US cost for its strikes on Ukraine’s grid. Protecting and restoring the grid falls to Ukraine’s air defenses and repair crews.
Russia hit energy sites 76 times in a week
Zelenskyy counted 76 deliberate Russian strikes on energy and oil-and-gas facilities since Trump’s announcement. Overnight, Russia hit substations in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa oblasts, he said. In the past week, Russia fired almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic, mainly to cause a blackout. His message was aimed at Washington.
“America must see that Russia is not taking steps in return for the lifting of sanctions or deals. On the contrary, they take every signal that they can make money as proof that their bet on war is working and they can keep fighting,” Zelenskyy wrote.
22 House lawmakers press Trump to implement Russia sanctions law. Diesel deal draws bipartisan backlash
Overnight, Russia launched one Iskander-M ballistic missile and 180 Shahed-type drones, 26 of them jet-powered, the Air Force reported. Air defenses downed or suppressed 152 drones, but strikes hit 20 locations.
Power cuts from Odesa to Ternopil
Strikes left about 24,000 consumers in Odesa Oblast without power, oblast head Oleh Kiper said. In Vinnytsia Oblast, the attack damaged critical infrastructure and forced emergency outages, oblast head Natalia Zabolotna wrote. Drones hit three energy facilities in Ternopil Oblast, one of them for the second time, and cut power to some consumers, oblast head Taras Pastukh said.
Civilians killed and injured
A Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia killed a 27-year-old woman and injured two others, including a 16-year-old, the State Emergency Service reported. In Poltava, an evening attack killed one person, injured four, and damaged 10 detached houses, city council secretary Kateryna Yamshchykova said.
Five Russian bombs kill 17 in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia next day after Trump lets Russia ship first 300,000 tonnes of its diesel
A drone hit a high-rise in Odesa and set its roof on fire. A 13-year-old girl was hurt, city military administration head Serhii Lysak said, and Kiper put the number of injured at two.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russian drones and artillery injured three people, oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha said. In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed seven civilians on Saturday, six of them in Sloviansk, oblast head Vadym Filashkin reported.
Fires in the west, alerts across the border
A morning drone strike set warehouse and production buildings ablaze at an enterprise in Manevychi, Volyn Oblast, oblast head Roman Romaniuk said. With heavy smoke blowing toward the town, Romaniuk urged residents to stay indoors, shut windows and doors, and switch off ventilation. A repeat strike set an enterprise in the district on fire again, the State Emergency Service said, adding that air tests found no dangerous concentrations outside the site. In Lviv Oblast, drone debris damaged a logistics warehouse and two houses, oblast head Maksym Kozytskyi said.
Polish military aircraft operated in Poland’s airspace twice during the attack, as the Government Security Centre warned residents of Lublin Voivodeship and later alerted Subcarpathian Voivodeship. In Lithuania, NATO jets failed to identify an object that apparently entered from Poland, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said.
A ceasefire Moscow never confirmed
Trump announced the energy ceasefire on 11 October, news that surprised Zelenskyy. A White House official said Russia was still weighing it. Hours later, Russia hit a Kharkiv power plant, and on 14 October it fired 39 ballistic missiles at the grid. Then Trump waived Graham Act penalties on buyers of Russian oil, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration wants 60 days to weigh the economic effects.

articles.title: Ukrainian drone attack causes fire at oil terminal in St. Petersburg
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone attack causes fire at oil terminal in St. Petersburg
A blaze has broken out at an oil terminal in St. Petersburg as a result of a major Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s second-largest city, local governor Aleksandr Beglov has said.
One person was killed and five others wounded in St. Petersburg during the aerial raid by “the Ukrainian Nazis,” Beglov said in a social media post on Sunday. Twelve apartment blocks and two private homes sustained damage, with repairs already being underway, he added.
Emergencies services have been tackling fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal in the Great Port of St. Petersburg, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses in Kolpinsky District, the governor said.
The affected oil terminal is the largest facility of its kind in the Baltic Region, handling 125 million tons of liquefied product per year.
Ukraine continues to target Russian oil infrastructure despite demands by US President Donald Trump to curb the attacks, which he blames for surging global energy prices. He accused Vladimir Zelensky of “making problems” for the US and the whole world and suggested that Ukraine needs a “new president.”
In an attempt to alleviate the fuel shortage ahead of the midterm election on November 3, Trump eased restrictions on Moscow’s diesel exports and waived “the bone-crushing” sanctions championed by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, which proposed 500% tariffs on imports from Russia and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
Flights have been delayed at St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo International Airport due to the raid, according to Beglov.
At least 144 UAVs were shot down by air defenses overnight, Aleksandr Drozdenko, the head of Leningrad Region, which surrounds St. Petersburg, said on social media.
Four people have been hospitalized for smoke inhalation from a blaze caused when debris from an intercepted UAV fell on an apartment block in the town of Vsevolzhsk, he said.
Residential areas were also hit by debris in Gatchina, Kirovsk and several other settlements, according to Drozdenko.
Some 20,000 people remain without electricity in Leningrad Region; two transformer substations in the community of Yanino, servicing some 50 apartment blocks, went offline during the Ukrainian raid, the governor said.
Russia’s leading social media platform VK said in a statement that one of its data centers in Leningrad Region has been targeted by Ukrainian UAVs.
According to the Downdetector website, the number of reports from users about issues with VK’s services increased following the attack.
The major Russian online retailer Ozon said that one of its warehouses was attacked during the raid. There were no injuries, as staff were evacuated, according to the company.
The Russian Defense Ministry has said that a total of 1,015 Ukrainian drones were destroyed above 16 regions overnight.
Moscow has accused Kiev of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure and residential areas with long-range drones in an attempt to compensate for setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces have continued to advance.
Russia has responded to Kiev’s terrorist attacks by intensifying its long-range missile and drone campaign against Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities and logistics infrastructure. The Defense Ministry in Moscow maintains that it does not target civilians and that its strikes are directed solely at military targets and infrastructure supporting Kiev’s forces.

articles.title: 4 New Air Defense Towers Built Near Putin’s Valdai Residence
articles.body:
Four additional air defense towers have been erected near the Valdai residence of Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Novgorod region of Russia, with the closest structure situated roughly 400 meters from the main residential compound, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Russian service reported.
Satellite imagery analyzed by investigative journalists revealed that the newly constructed elevated platforms expand an already dense protective perimeter surrounding the presidential retreat.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
With the addition of the four new towers, the total number of specialized air defense towers identified in the immediate vicinity of the Valdai compound has grown to approximately 30.
The installation of elevated ramparts and stationary towers across Russian territory is engineered primarily to host short-range surface-to-air missile and anti-aircraft artillery systems, such as the Pantsir-S1, elevating radar and kinetic engagement equipment above regional forest canopies to detect and intercept low-altitude strike drones.
The Valdai estate, located on Lake Valdai approximately midway between Moscow and St. Petersburg, serves as a heavily fortified private retreat frequented by Putin and his inner circle.
White House Defends Russia Sanctions Waiver to Aid Peace Talks
Expanding multi-layered perimeter around Valdai
The construction of the four new towers marks the latest phase in a progressive militarization of the airspace safeguarding the presidential retreat against asymmetric Ukrainian drone incursions.
In early April, investigative reports based on satellite imagery confirmed that Russian engineering units had completed seven new stationary air defense towers mounting Pantsir systems around the Valdai complex between late 2025 and March 2026.
Over subsequent months, secondary rings of fortified positions were established along surrounding access routes and peripheral forested areas.
Concurrently, Russian security agencies reinforced ground-level defenses around the complex. In early June, independent Russian media outlets, including Meduza and Agentstvo, verified the installation of anti-drone netting systems over transport routes and truck staging facilities in the Valdai district, approximately nine kilometers (5.6 miles) from the compound.
Defense analysts from the Conflict Intelligence Team (CIT) observed that the netting arrays – technologies widely employed along frontline sectors in Ukraine to shield vehicles from loitering munitions and first-person view (FPV) drone drops – were deployed around Valdai to protect security convoys and control access corridors amid Ukraine’s expanding long-range drone campaign.
Concentric air defense rings around Moscow
The continuous reinforcement of the Valdai residence forms part of a broader, systemic effort by Russian defense planners to erect dense, layered air defense networks around high-value leadership compounds, strategic command hubs, and the Russian capital.
In late June, satellite reconnaissance revealed that Russian forces established a fortified S-400 long-range surface-to-air missile position fewer than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) from the Kremlin in western Moscow.
Constructed across a 4.5-hectare concrete platform near Moscow State University’s Innovation Science and Technology Center – the flagship project of the Innopraktika Foundation directed by Putin’s daughter Kateryna Tikhonova – the site incorporates S-300 and S-400 missile launchers alongside a 40V6MR mobile radar mast designed to detect low-flying aerodynamic targets.

articles.title: Sybiha: 76 Energy Strikes Prove Moscow Flouts Ceasefire
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has warned that Russia is systematically expandeing targeted strikes against Ukraine’s power grid while feigning interest in diplomatic initiatives, stating that 76 targeted attacks on energy infrastructure over the past week prove Moscow has honored no commitments.
Writing on X on Sunday, Oct. 18, Sybiha stressed that offering economic accommodations or easing sanctions under such conditions only equips the Kremlin with fresh revenue to underwrite ongoing military operations ahead of winter.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Its message could hardly be clearer – Moscow has not abided by any obligations,” Sybiha stated, noting that tens of thousands of Ukrainian families remain without electricity as international partners attempt to explore avenues to conclude the war.
The foreign minister reiterated figures disclosed earlier in the day by President Volodymyr Zelensky, pointing out that Russian forces carried out 76 targeted attacks against Ukrainian energy facilities since US President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” one week ago.
Sybiha added that over the preceding seven days alone, Russian forces deployed nearly 2,700 strike drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs (KABs), and 66 missiles across Ukrainian territory, with the vast majority of missile systems consisting of high-speed ballistic weapons directed at municipal utilities.
US Tech Curbs on Kyiv Expose Allied Dependency
Simulated diplomacy and economic pressure
Ukraine’s top diplomat observed that the Kremlin is pursuing an asymmetric strategy engineered to secure international sanctions relief without altering its operational conduct or military objectives on the ground.
According to Sybiha, Moscow seeks “sanctions relief without changing its behavior, preservation of profits without accountability, and the imitation of diplomatic efforts without any commitment to stop killing Ukrainians.”
Addressing international allies and policymakers in Washington, Sybiha cautioned that lowering the economic costs of Russian aggression while civilian infrastructure faces daily bombardment directly undermines prospective peace efforts.
“Easing economic pressure under these circumstances risks giving the Kremlin additional resources to finance its war,” Sybiha emphasized.
“It is time for our partners to draw the necessary conclusions. Any serious effort to end this war must increase pressure on Moscow, restrict the revenues financing its aggression, and strengthen Ukraine’s ability to defend its cities and energy infrastructure.”
The foreign minister underlined that Russia bears unilateral responsibility for prolonging the conflict, dismissing the notion that commercial accommodations can incentivize de-escalation.
“Reducing the cost of its aggression while it continues attacking Ukraine will not bring peace,” Sybiha concluded. “It can only make further aggression easier to finance.”
Sanctions waivers and energy armistice disputes
Sybiha’s public remarks arrive amid sharp transatlantic disagreements over the Trump administration’s recent foreign policy maneuvers toward Moscow.
On Friday, Oct. 16, Trump signed an executive order invoking Section 115 of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 to waive mandatory statutory penalties, including 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports and 100 percent duties targeting global purchasers of Russian hydrocarbons, just 48 hours before their scheduled implementation.
The waiver follows an Oct. 9 bilateral commercial arrangement between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, under which Moscow agreed to deliver refined diesel onto international markets through 2027 to curb fuel benchmark inflation.
The shipments were authorized under a general license issued by the US Treasury Department.
While White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers argued that enforcing statutory sanctions now would impede ongoing diplomatic efforts to broker a peace settlement, Ukrainian officials have strongly contested that assessment.
Both Zelensky and Sybiha have warned that granting Moscow access to international energy markets injects direct hard currency into the Russian state budget during active military operations, validating the Kremlin’s calculation that its war effort is yielding economic dividends rather than consequences.

articles.title: Intensifying drone attacks on ships in Black Sea bring war ever closer to Nato shores
articles.body:
The first the crew of the Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria knew of an attack on a cargo ship in their country’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea in the early hours of 6 October was a distant explosion 70 miles off the coastal town of Byala.
The Turkish-owned Alfa Watan, heading for the Romanian port of Sulina, had been struck by suspected Russian air and naval drones. Arriving on the scene, Dioscuria found an overturned lifeboat and lifejackets in the water. There was no sign, however, of Alfa Watan’s crew of 10.
Six days later drones struck another ship off the coast of Bulgaria, HS Dignity. Eleven crew members died.
By Thursday, the attacks had encroached on Romania’s airspace and territorial water. Two chemical tankers, Wine Trader and Yara J, were attacked and left burning. Seven more sailors were missing.
The attacks on six ships in 10 days – the Able and Chelsea-3 were also hit – marked a dramatic escalation in a maritime conflict that is pressing on Nato’s borders.
While global attention has focused on the risks for sailors travelling through the strait of Hormuz, in recent months it is the Black Sea that has emerged as the more dangerous passage, with more sailors lost in a week and a half than US service members killed in the entire Iran war.
The maritime insurer and risk analyst Ambrey has warned that there is no end in sight to the threats to Black Sea cargo shipping, including grain and oil, and that insurance prices for passage of the waters have rocketed.
Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey, has noted a sharp increase in the tempo of attacks beginning in July. Russian forces are estimated to be responsible for 80% of them.
The recent loss of life, he suggests, has been exacerbated by “double tap” attacks involving aerial and surface drones, the latter often carrying up to half a tonne of explosive payloads. Smaller vessels that primarily use the Danube canal system have sunk rapidly.
“While attacks against merchant vessels in the Black Sea are not new, we are seeing an escalation both in terms of the number of attacks and in the geographical scope,” Alexa said.
The profile of vessels being attacked – that is, ships trading with Ukraine – had not changed, he added. “The Russian intent is clear, which is to degrade the export of Ukrainian grain and agricultural products.”
The result has been a precipitous fall in the number of vessels visiting Ukraine. Insurance rates have soared, and seafarers and operators have become increasingly reluctant to operate in the Black Sea basin, even on ships unconnected with Ukrainian cargoes.
The vast majority of the more than 60 fatalities of seafarers in the Black Sea since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 have occurred in the past year. In September the Joint War Committee, representing the London insurance market, moved to extend the high-risk areas of the Black Sea to include the whole of the basin, excluding the territorial waters of Turkey, Romania, Bulgaria and Georgia.
The threat is not confined to the Black Sea itself. Attacks on Ukraine’s Black Sea ports have also increased sharply in the past year.
A number of factors are driving the expansion and escalation of the conflict towards the shores of Nato countries, say experts. Russia has responded to a geographical expansion of Ukrainian strikes on its shadow fleet of oil tankers by intensifying strikes on Ukrainian agricultural cargoes – a key component of Kyiv’s economy.
As ships sought safer passage further from the coastlines, so the threat has changed: from naval mines to drones, with ever longer ranges.
Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, said after the sinking of the Alfa Watan: “Commercial ships – and innocent crews – are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea.”
In a statement at the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, Col Joby Rimmer, a senior British military adviser, said: “Attacks that fail to distinguish between military objectives and civilian vessels, or that are expected to cause excessive incidental harm to civilians and civilian vessels in relation to the anticipated military advantage, may violate international humanitarian law and the UN convention on the law of the sea.
“Each attack raises the risk to crews of every nationality, drives up insurance costs and restricts the flow of food to those who depend on it. The UK is deeply concerned by the far-reaching consequences of successive crises across the global maritime domain. Stable and secure sea lanes are a global common good from which we all benefit.”
Operators have warned of the wider impact on trade in the Black Sea, including from Bulgarian ports. In a recent interview on Bulgarian television, the shipping agency owner Todor Georgiev warned the Black Sea was in danger of becoming a “dead zone”.
“Whenever the Russians are caught having struck a ship with one of their drones, they claim the vessel was carrying weapons,” he said. “Weapons are not being transported to Ukraine via the Black Sea.”
Rumen Radev, Bulgaria’s prime minister, has described the attacks in the vicinity of his country’s territorial waters as “absolutely unacceptable”.
Bulgarian officials are calling for the EU and Nato to support the efforts to enhance security, while working with Turkey and Romania on increased regional security.
Although they have refused to attribute blame to Russia, officials have said there is “no logic” for Ukraine to attack its own shipments.
“We do not have clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility to either side,” said Radev. “However, as I have already stated, the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation.”
As Russian strikes on shipping move ever closer to the borders of Nato members, they pose mounting security challenges to the mutual defence organisation, which is already confronting Moscow’s growing hybrid warfare across Europe. There is speculation that the affected Nato countries may be forced to invoke article 4 of the organisation’s treaty, a step below the article 5 invocation of mutual self defence.
Triggered twice already around the Ukraine war – in the immediate aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and by Poland in 2025 after Russian drones violated Warsaw’s airspace – it calls for formal crisis discussions on a security threat.
On Thursday Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, met Radev and Nicușor Dan, Romania’s president, to discuss security in the Black Sea. Rutte said: “Nato will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed.”
Another consequence of the escalating attacks is the renewed danger of a global food crisis. Ukraine and Russia are major exporters of grain, as is Romania.
“We’re looking at the Black Sea as a global food artery,” said Oana Toiu, the Romanian foreign minister, at a security conference in Warsaw last week. “It is currently, unfortunately, the deadliest sea when it comes to the number of casualties of sailors in the last months. That means we need to increase our investments in deterrence, defence.”
Damien Chevallier, the director of maritime safety at the UN’s International Maritime Organization, warned last month of the long-term impact on shipping caused by attacks linked to the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.
“With rising casualties across the Black Sea, Red Sea and strait of Hormuz, being a seafarer has become a genuinely dangerous profession,” he said. “Seafarers are not trained to deal with threats from actions which are linked to wider security issues or geopolitical situations.
“What makes this moment genuinely unprecedented is not just the number of incidents, but the pattern behind them. Shipping has become a deliberate instrument of geopolitical leverage.”

articles.title: Latvia’s combat-tested ground drone shows off in Finland
articles.body:
- Latvian company NATRIX demonstrated its combat-tested unmanned ground vehicle at Millog’s UGV Demo 2026 in Mikkeli, Finland, on Oct. 8.
- The vehicle showed forest mobility, obstacle crossing, cargo transport and remote control before Finnish military, border guard and police officials.
Latvian company NATRIX, already a supplier of ground drones to Latvia’s armed forces, showed its battle-tested unmanned ground vehicle to Finnish military and security officials on Oct. 8, driving it through forest terrain and hauling cargo at an unmanned ground systems demonstration in Mikkeli, Finland.
The event was organized by Millog, the Finnish defense maintenance company that services much of the Finnish Defence Forces’ equipment, and brought together several manufacturers of ground drones. NATRIX attended with its Finnish partner Armatech Finland, the company said in a LinkedIn post, and showed the vehicle to representatives from several branches of the Finnish Defence Forces, the Finnish Ministry of Defence, the Finnish Border Guard, the Police of Finland and international military delegations.
In its live demonstration, NATRIX said the vehicle showed its mobility and ability to cross obstacles in rough forest terrain, carried cargo, and was driven remotely by an operator. The company also briefed visitors on lessons from the platform’s use in combat.
The NATRIX UGV is a compact, battery-powered vehicle built for front-line resupply, casualty evacuation and reconnaissance support. The company says it can carry more than 200 kg (440 pounds) of cargo and can be fitted with a NATO-standard stretcher to bring out wounded troops, and that its communications use several backup channels to stay connected in jammed environments.
The platform began combat testing in Ukraine’s Donbas region in early 2025, after the first vehicles were funded through a donation campaign run by Latvian public media and the Ziedot.lv charity platform. Co-founder Gatis Vectirāns said at the time that a fully charged vehicle could travel about 20 km (12 miles), and that Ukrainian operators had praised its power and build quality, Latvian public broadcaster LSM reported.
In April 2026, Latvia’s Ministry of Defence signed contracts with NATRIX and two other Latvian companies, Brasa Defence Systems and LV-Teh, to supply domestically made ground drones and gradually introduce them into regular units of the National Armed Forces, The Defence Blog reported. The deals followed live demonstrations on military training ranges in 2025 and include support, repair and modernization, as well as the right for Latvia to order more systems quickly under the same framework.
Ukraine now relies heavily on ground drones to move ammunition, food and water to positions where Russian surveillance drones make vehicle and foot traffic dangerous, and to evacuate wounded soldiers under fire. Finland, which shares a 1,340 km (830-mile) border with Russia, has been studying those lessons as it expands its own forces.
NATRIX is developing autonomous features such as “follow me” and automatic return modes and plans to add mine-clearing equipment and weapon integration. Last month the company also unveiled a separate ground drone designed to patrol critical infrastructure such as energy sites, ports and airports, and it said the Mikkeli demonstration opened talks with Finnish defense and security officials on possible future cooperation.

articles.title: Iranian fishermen scramble for loot from sunken container ship after explosion
articles.body:
The Persian Gulf coast in Iran became the scene of unusual activity this week as local fishermen abandoned their traditional fishing nets and headed into the waters of the Strait of Hormuz in small motorboats and rescue dinghies with one clear goal: to collect valuable cargo floating on the water's surface.
According to a report by The Telegraph, a massive shipment containing hundreds of brand-new iPhones, luxury French perfumes, and other consumer goods spilled into the sea following the sinking of the container ship "GFS Pride" on October 14.
Videos circulating on social media show dozens of local fishermen navigating between semi-submerged containers while pulling boxes directly from the waves, with one small boat even seen attempting to tow a fully loaded giant shipping container.
Authorities in Singapore, where the vessel is flagged, confirmed that the ship sank following a fire that broke out on deck, but all 21 crew members were evacuated unharmed.
Conversely, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy claimed that the vessel strayed into an "unauthorized and dangerous" lane and struck a naval mine, which sank it along with more than 2,500 containers on board. This is the third vessel to sink in the area since the outbreak of hostilities in late February.
Surge of hostile IRGC activity in the Strait of Hormuz
This incident occurs against the backdrop of a sharp surge in hostile IRGC activity surrounding the strategic strait.
Last Friday, Iranian armed forces spokesman Gen. Mohammad Akraminia clarified that the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon a full withdrawal of United States forces from the region, threatening that Iranian forces would forcibly expel American troops if they remained.
According to him, foreign presence in the area undermines maritime security, and he urged shipowners to utilize only corridors supervised by the Iranian military to ensure their safety.
Maritime and land warfare in the region continues unabated. The Iranian Navy reported closely monitoring a fire that broke out aboard an oil tanker in the Gulf of Oman after it attempted to cross a "prohibited zone" while turning off its tracking systems.
On the other side of the Arabian Peninsula, the Houthi movement in Yemen tightened its siege on the city of Taiz, while the Saudi-led coalition announced it successfully intercepted and destroyed ballistic missiles and drones launched toward Riyadh and Red Sea ports.

articles.title: Rubio: Ukraine Does Not Have Access to Starshield
articles.body:
Ukraine currently lacks access to the specialized military-grade Starshield satellite network and has requested the technology to conduct deep-interdiction strikes inside Russia, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.
Speaking to journalists in comments released by the US Department of State, Rubio clarified the distinction between SpaceX’s standard commercial Starlink communications framework and the dedicated Starshield architecture operated under contract with the US Department of Defense.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Starlink is a commercial product, okay? And so it’s regulated and handled as a commercial product. Starshield is a defense product, a military product,” Rubio stated.
“That is something that the United States military uses. It’s not at this moment available to Ukraine, and that’s under conversation. It’s under discussion right now how they would want to use it.”
Responding to questions regarding reports of technological throttling, Rubio directly refuted claims that the Trump administration had mandated bandwidth or velocity caps on terminals operating in Ukrainian combat sectors.
“I know Ukraine wants access to Starshield. They do not have Starshield now. They’ve asked for access to it in order to conduct deep strikes inside of Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment,” Rubio emphasized.
“Those are two different products.”
Zelensky Calls Trump’s Sanctions Waiver a Mistake
White House denies intentional velocity caps
Rubio pushed back against assertions by President Volodymyr Zelensky that artificial operational constraints imposed on Starlink terminals inside Ukraine were deliberate administrative measures.
“I don’t know what Zelensky said. I’m not sure Zelensky knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate. We have nothing to do with that,” Rubio said.
“Nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it’s been restored. It’s back to where it was before. That’s Starlink, though. They were using Starlink for their drones.”
Addressing media reports suggesting executive coordination to limit unmanned systems, the secretary of state characterized the allegations as completely unfounded.
“Nothing to do with the White House. I saw a report on that the other day. It’s just categorically false,” Rubio told reporters.
“No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it. But my understanding is it’s back up and running. That’s what I read – that’s what we heard two days ago.”
Zelensky’s 161 km/h disclosure
Rubio’s comments follow detailed disclosures delivered on Saturday, Oct. 17, by President Zelensky, who revealed that Starlink terminals operating inside Ukrainian territory had been subjected to a strict velocity limitation of 161 km/h (100 mph).
According to Zelensky, whenever equipped domestic platforms exceeded the 161 km/h threshold, satellite connections automatically severed, causing operators to lose control of unmanned interceptors in mid-flight.
The velocity cap effectively disabled domestic drone interceptors tasked with neutralizing high-speed, turbojet-powered Russian Shahed loitering munitions, which penetrate sovereign airspace at speeds exceeding 400 km/h (250 mph).
Zelensky highlighted that Ukrainian technical teams conducted cross-border comparative evaluations, sending Starlink-equipped vehicles into EU territory, where the devices operated uninterrupted at velocities of 180 km/h (112 mph). The Ukrainian leader argued that the trials confirmed the restrictions were geographically targeted at Ukrainian airspace rather than stemming from global software glitches.
The Starshield controversy
The technological dispute underscores widening geopolitical friction between Washington and Kyiv over long-range interdiction limits and commercial communications dependencies.
Rubio’s denials echo statements by US President Donald Trump, who told that neither he nor SpaceX founder Elon Musk ordered operational caps on Ukraine’s military communications, asserting that “everything is the same as it’s always been.”
However, both official denials contradict reporting by The Telegraph, which cited four sources familiar with the matter stating that Musk directly proposed satellite service limitations to Trump, who approved the measure, clearing the way for the Pentagon to restrict Starshield functionality.
Sources cited in the report claimed Musk sought to shift public accountability onto the White House amid concerns over potential consumer boycotts across European markets following civilian casualties in Kyiv.
