articles.title: Israel must treat the media war as seriously as Iran’s nuclear threat, Gil Hoffman says
articles.body:
Three years after Hamas’s October 7 attack, Israel is still fighting a war it was never prepared for, one in which the weapons are not missiles or tanks but headlines, social media posts, and the narratives that shape how the world sees the Jewish state.
For Gil Hoffman, a veteran political analyst who has spent much of his career examining how Israel is portrayed abroad, this battle is not simply a public relations issue, but a strategic threat that the country’s leadership has repeatedly failed to recognize.
Hoffman covered politics for The Jerusalem Post for nearly a quarter century, before taking over as executive director and executive editor of HonestReporting to “lead the fight for Israel on the media battlefield.”
He spoke with the Post this week in the wake of the publication of his new book, The Blood Libel Machine, which argues that the spread of anti-Israel narratives and the surge in global antisemitism were not simply spontaneous responses to the war, but the result of a premeditated information campaign that had been in the works for decades.
On October 7, 2023, that media battlefield took on a new urgency. As Hamas terrorists crossed into southern Israel, the images and accounts of the massacre spread quickly around the world.
Israel failed on a major front: The media landscape
Hoffman saw that Israel had been caught off guard in two distinct but interconnected arenas. In his book, he describes October 7 as not only a military and intelligence failure, but also a failure on the media front.
Three years on, he said, Israel still fundamentally misunderstands how to communicate with the world.
Israel’s failure to prepare for the media battlefield
“Hamas planned this war in order to impact public opinion around the world,” he said. “Their goal was not Nova, which they did not know about; it was New York, and Israel played into their hands. They wanted Israel to respond with what they could call disproportionate force, no matter what it would be, and return the Palestinian issue to the international agenda.”
Israel not having a plan on this front, just like it didn’t have a plan on the military front, has harmed the Jewish state “tremendously,” Hoffman added.
“Every day since October 7 has become easier on the military battlefield. Every day since October 7 has gotten progressively harder on the media one.”
The contrast is central to his book. Israel has devoted enormous resources to its military prowess, but Hoffman argues that successive governments have treated public diplomacy as a secondary concern, despite its potential influence on both domestic security and the security of Jewish communities abroad.
According to Hoffman, the problem begins at the highest levels of government.
“They did not realize they need to be taking into account how the decision they’re about to make in Gaza, in Iran, against Hezbollah, how these decisions are going to impact the Jews in Golders Green and in New York. They did not take it into account whatsoever.”
Another strategic failure Hoffman identified is Israel’s tendency to remain on the defensive rather than challenge the credibility and motivations of those shaping the international narrative.
Much of Israel’s media strategy, if there is one, has focused on rebutting misinformation, disputing facts and figures, and pointing out flaws in logic.
Hoffman said Israel needs to be much more on the offensive.
In his book, he lays out four necessary strategies he believes must work together: offensive and defensive messaging, both within the context of the conflict and beyond it.
“I count four. It makes a Venn diagram that works all together. If you’re missing out on any of the four, then it’s inadequate. So, yes, we need to be blackening the names of the people fighting against us.”
For example, Israel should be “outing” international anti-Israel figures who are accepting huge amounts of money from Qatar, Hoffman argued.
“We need to be outing that. It’s not legitimate, the way that Qatar is influencing the world. Al Jazeera is not a legitimate news organization. It’s a propaganda mouthpiece of a terrorist-supporting state. People need to know that. People need to know what they can and they can’t trust.”
Qatar occupies a prominent place in Hoffman’s analysis. The Gulf state, which has hosted Hamas political leaders and played a central role in negotiations involving Israel and Hamas, funds Al Jazeera, one of the most influential Arabic-language news networks in the world. Hoffman argues that Qatar’s financial and media influence warrants greater scrutiny.
The offensive strategy also needs to be employed more on college campuses, where, for a very long time, the pro-Israel groups have been trying to be “nice,” and Hoffman says they “need to be less nice because the anti-Israel organizations on their campus are not nice.”
He believes pro-Israel students and organizations need to be more assertive in challenging anti-Israel activism rather than relying primarily on dialogue and attempts to persuade those already strongly opposed to Israel.
This also connects to Qatar, given the extensive reporting indicating significant academic institutional ties between the Gulf state and US universities.
How international institutions shape the narrative
One of the most challenging aspects of this media fight is combating the dominant narrative disseminated by human rights bodies and NGOs, Hoffman said.
The United Nations, Oxfam, Amnesty International, Doctors Without Borders, and others have been instrumental in legitimizing the anti-Israel rhetoric used in public and private spaces. Because of these organizations, buzzwords such as “genocide,” “apartheid,” and “ethnic cleansing” have become normalized in day-to-day discourse and in international media outlets.
Hoffman said he wanted to speak to journalists who covered the conflict during the war and “give them the benefit of the doubt.” He said he asked them why they believed Hamas.
“They said, ‘No, we didn’t believe anything from Hamas. We believe the organizations [like the UN].’ And they believed Hamas.
“These organizations were the ones who spread the propaganda and sanitized what a terrorist organization [Hamas] told them. Then the media quote these reputable organizations around the world, and it becomes a vicious circle. As Gerald Steinberg, the founder of NGO Monitor, understood way back at the Durban [Conference], this was going to cause damage to Israel, and now the entire world needs to understand that.”
The Durban reference is significant. At the 2001 UN World Conference Against Racism in South Africa, an accompanying NGO forum became the focus of controversy over antisemitism and the portrayal of Israel. Its declaration described Israel as an apartheid state and accused it of genocide and ethnic cleansing, language that would become increasingly prominent in subsequent campaigns against the Jewish state.
In Hoffman’s view, the events surrounding Durban were not an isolated episode but an early indication of how human rights terminology could be used as part of a broader campaign to delegitimize Israel.
“So, that’s part of that blood libel machine, the way in which – wittingly or unwittingly, and, unfortunately, too often wittingly – these NGOs were part of it. So the blood libel machine is the media. It is Qatar. It is Hamas. It is the anti-Israel organizations around the world.”
Fighting back against the machine
Fighting this is an uphill battle, partly because these organizations are viewed internationally as the beacons of justice and paragons of morality. It is not easy to convince skeptics that their findings and public statements should be subjected to the same scrutiny as those of governments and other parties.
“It’s hard, but we need to be constantly putting out facts,” Hoffman continued. “We know how many tons of aid we’re giving to Gaza. We know what everything Israel did unprecedentedly to help an enemy combatant in the time of war. We know how much effort Israel made to minimize civilian casualties. Little by little, we can chisel away at this false narrative that has been hoisted upon the world.”
Hoffman’s determination to remain optimistic is a recurring theme throughout both the book and the interview, even as he describes the scale of the challenge facing Israel.
“I didn’t want to write a book of gloom and doom. I wanted to write a book that would give people hope.
“That’s why the subtitle of the book is Exposing the anti-Israel Hate Network, and How to Fight Back. I give people 30 different tools they can use, whether it’s in mainstream media, social media, or AI platforms.”
Rather than leaving readers with a diagnosis of the problem, Hoffman devotes a substantial portion of the book to practical action. He does not believe it is too late for Israel to turn the tide.
“It’s not too late. Every day, every single person on social media and even people who aren’t on social media, in the checkout line of the grocery store, everybody can make an impact.
“I don’t view it as this mountain that’s insurmountable. I believe in celebrating incremental success. And we, every day, can change minds. Not of the most extreme people, but of the overwhelming majority.”
One way he suggests people take action is by engaging more critically with international media and holding them accountable when they find incorrect or biased reporting.
“People often ask me, should I cancel my subscription to The New York Times and other media outlets for being anti-Israel?
“I say absolutely not. You need to be reading it. If you want to hurt them, then read them more carefully. If you see something problematic, send it to the media watchdogs like HonestReporting or to journalists themselves, or send it to their local media and point out that their rival had made an error. And that’s all part of regaining deterrence on the media battlefield.”
This approach is shaped by his years in journalism and media monitoring. Rather than disengage from outlets they distrust, Hoffman argues, readers should become more informed, attentive consumers of their reporting.
He cited an example of when, during coverage of the release of the final 20 living hostages in October 2025, CNN reporter Christiane Amanpour claimed that Israeli hostages were treated “better than the average Gazan” because Hamas used them as bargaining chips.
Someone flagged the comment, and Hoffman himself then contacted Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, who contacted CNN and requested that she be held accountable.
Amanpour subsequently apologized, calling her comments insensitive and wrong.
“That came from ordinary people who were watching and made sure that we would realize this. And so people can have that role when they see things that are egregious.”
Social media also has the technology for users to critically engage. For example, users on X/Twitter can add community notes on posts that are incorrectly presented or are missing key information.
Looking to Israel’s next government
While Hoffman does believe responsibility can rest with individual news consumers, his criticism ultimately returns to Israel’s political leadership and its failure to treat public diplomacy as an essential element of national security.
While citizens may help challenge misleading narratives, only the government has the authority and tools to establish a coordinated, long-term communications strategy, one that anticipates the international consequences of its actions rather than responding after the damage has been done.
“They need to be taking this just as seriously as the nuclear threat from Iran, because it’s an existential threat to the future of the State of Israel and the Jewish people around the world.
“And they need to be caring about the way every decision they make is perceived abroad.”
With Israel’s October 27 elections approaching, the question is whether a new government, regardless of its political makeup, will be prepared to invest in the media battlefield as seriously as it invests in conventional security.
“It doesn’t matter who wins the election. They all need to make sure the next government allocates just as much, if not more, funding to media strategy and public diplomacy. They need to have people ready 24/7 to go on the media and explain what’s going on here, in every language imaginable.
“The embassies and consulates abroad are dreadfully underfunded. And that needs to be changed, because those are the people who are building the relationships with the people there on the ground and with the media.”
Hoffman makes the case that the fight over Israel’s international reputation will not end when the fighting on the ground does. It will continue in newsrooms, universities, online platforms, and in day-to-day communication.
And while governments bear the most responsibility for preparing Israel to confront that challenge, Hoffman’s resounding message is that the battlefield is no longer theirs alone. Its outcome will also depend on whether those watching from the sidelines are willing to take action.

articles.title: U.S. Army tests Ukrainian uncrewed surface vessels as drone carriers
articles.body:
- Ukrainian-built Magura drone boats took part in the U.S. Army’s Bayonet Quest 26 exercise in Michigan, launching aerial drones from a platform on the hull.
- The same boat family sank a target ship during Balikatan 2026 in the Philippines on April 24, 2026.
Ukraine’s Magura uncrewed surface vessels, the drone boats that have sunk Russian warships in the Black Sea, took part in a U.S. Army exercise in Michigan, where they were used as floating launch pads for aerial drones.
The boats appeared during Bayonet Quest 26, which the 7th Infantry Division, part of Multi-Domain Command-Pacific, ran across Michigan from Sept. 26 to Oct. 6, 2026. The division said soldiers used the exercise to test autonomous systems and uncrewed aircraft as it experiments with how new technology can extend sensing, reach and decision-making.
According to images and materials released by the division, the exercise included crewed-uncrewed maritime testing that paired a Mk VI patrol boat with autonomous systems, giving the U.S. Army a look at how the two could work together in complex terrain. The Magura boats, built by Ukrainian manufacturer UFORCE, carried a dedicated platform on the front of the hull from which aerial drones took off.
The 7th Infantry Division did not say how many Magura boats took part, which model was used, or what type of aerial drones they carried.
The Michigan exercise is the second publicly known use of the Magura family by U.S. forces this year. During Balikatan 2026, the largest annual U.S.-Philippines military exercise, Magura boats destroyed a decommissioned target ship in a live-fire maritime strike off Itbayat in the Batanes islands on April 24, 2026. UFORCE confirmed on June 8 that its vessels had taken part, after The Defence Blog reported that U.S. special forces had sunk a ship with Ukrainian-designed drone boats.
Magura boats became one of Ukraine’s best-known weapons after its military intelligence used them to strike Russian Black Sea Fleet ships near Crimea, forcing much of the fleet to move away from the peninsula. Ukraine has since developed versions armed with missiles and machine guns, and in 2025 Ukrainian military intelligence said Magura boats armed with air-to-air missiles had shot down Russian fighter jets over the Black Sea.
Using a drone boat to carry and launch aerial drones extends how far a small craft can see and strike without putting a crewed ship close to the target. Ukraine has used drone boats in a similar way to carry smaller strike drones toward Russian-held coastlines, and the U.S. Army has been looking at uncrewed boats for its units in the Pacific, where many operations would play out among islands and along coastlines.
The 7th Infantry Division, based at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state, was reorganized under Multi-Domain Command-Pacific as part of the U.S. Army’s efforts to prepare for operations in the Indo-Pacific region.

articles.title: ADF down 152 out of 180 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine
articles.body:
ADF down 152 out of 180 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine
As reported by Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on Saturday, October 17, the enemy attacked Ukraine with one Iskander-M ballistic missile launched from Russia’s Voronezh region, as well as 180 Shahed-type attack UAVs, 26 of them jet-powered, S-8000 Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones launched from the directions of Oryol, Bryansk, Kursk, Shatalovo and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by Ukrainian Air Defense Forces, surface-to-air missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire teams of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 8:00 on Sunday, October 18, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 152 enemy UAVs.
Hits by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at 20 locations, while downed drones and their debris fell at four locations.
The attack is ongoing. About 10 enemy UAVs remain in Ukrainian airspace.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Starlink operations in Ukraine are restricted to speeds of up to 161 km/h, making it impossible to use the system on interceptors designed to counter jet-powered Shahed drones.

articles.title: Rubio says Ukraine without access to Starshield, future ‘under discussion’
articles.body:
Rubio says Ukraine without access to Starshield, future ‘under discussion’
US secretary of state says Ukraine has requested access to military-grade version of Starlink for strikes deep inside Russia.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite service, is currently unavailable to Ukraine, but a request from Kyiv to access the system for attacks deep inside Russia is “under discussion”.
Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Rubio stressed Starshield’s distinction with Starlink, the internet service provided by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
“Starlink is a commercial product, okay? And so it’s regulated and handled as a commercial product. Starshield is a defence product, a military product,” said Rubio, in comments released by the Department of State.
“They’ve asked for access to it in order to conduct deep strikes inside of Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment,” he added. “That’s under conversation.”
Launched in 2022 and provided to the US government, Starshield is designed for military use as it allows for deeper encryption to process sensitive information. SpaceX says it is primarily used by US defence agencies and other “government partners”.
Last week, Ukrainian officials said restrictions on Starlink terminals had slowed some drones on the battlefield, as Ukraine tries to hold back Russian forces in their nearly five-year war.
In his comments at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, Rubio also rejected Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s suggestion that the reported disruption to Starlink services in Ukraine on Wednesday was deliberate.
“Well, I don’t know what Zelenskyy said. I’m not sure Zelenskyy knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate. We have nothing to do with that,” Rubio said.
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that the satellites are not tracking antennas on flying objects travelling faster than 161 kilometres per hour (100 miles per hour). This is affecting Ukrainian drones in their defence against Russian jet-powered drones and in their own medium-range attacks, he added.
Rubio said the US had not ordered Starlink speeds to be reduced and that the service had reportedly been restored to its previous level.
“No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it,” he said, calling the reports “categorically false”.
The remarks came as US President Donald Trump drew criticism from Democrats and Republicans after waiving sanctions on Russia and countries that buy its oil and gas, days before the restrictions were due to take effect under a law he signed last month.
Zelenskyy also criticised the sanctions waiver on Saturday, saying easing pressure on Russia would encourage further attacks.
“Financial rewards for [President Vladimir] Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” Zelenskyy posted on social media, urging the US to maintain pressure on Moscow.

articles.title: Zelenskyy warns Trump sanctions waiver risks fueling Russian aggression
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Saturday that U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to waive impending sanctions and tariffs on Russia would hand Moscow an economic reprieve and risk emboldening further Russian aggression.
"The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "It definitely helps only the Russians."
An executive order issued by Trump on Friday night waived key Russia-related U.S. sanctions and tariffs - including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas - that had been scheduled to start next week under the legislation known as the Graham Act that he signed into law last month.
Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the United States.
The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming toward Moscow while publicly criticizing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.
Zelenskyy said Trump's latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin and encourages more attacks by Russia.
"It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people," wrote Zelenskyy, who said Russia on Friday struck more than 15 Ukrainian power generation and transmission sites. "This certainly does not stop the war."
The Ukrainian leader accused Russia of planning to ramp up strikes in western Ukraine. "Is Russia preparing for this? I think so," Zelenskyy wrote.
Russia's investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, on Friday called the Trump waiver "a truly historic moment," posting on X that had the penalties taken effect, they could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a halt.
Weeks before U.S. midterm elections in which Trump's Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked further raising oil prices as Americans face increased costs largely attributed to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, analysts have said.
Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.
The legislation, whose primary backer in Congress was the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the U.S. from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.
Countries such as China and India, which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, however, had raised concerns about the Graham Act.
Beijing has said it "consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law" while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties.
But the Graham Act also allows the president to waive sanctions by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest. Friday's executive order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that "further action is appropriate."
U.S. Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said Trump was giving in to Putin.
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer said in a statement on Friday.
Graham, who died in July, strongly supported U.S. assistance to Ukraine. The passage of the bill named for him had provided hope that there would be continued bipartisan support for Kyiv, wrote Zelenskyy, who lamented the late senator's absence.
"It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest," Zelenskyy posted on Saturday.
The Ukrainian leader predicted that the U.S. under Trump will continue sanctions relief for Russia beyond Friday's waiver and the diesel export agreement announced earlier this month.
"I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately," Zelenskyy wrote.

articles.title: Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s St Petersburg kills 1, hits energy sites
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s St Petersburg kills 1, hits energy sites
Zelenskyy says Russian attacks on Ukraine overnight kill two people, adding Moscow continues to break energy ceasefire.
A “massive” Ukrainian drone attack on St Petersburg in Russia has killed at least one person and injured five others, the city’s governor said on Sunday.
Alexandre Beglov said firefighters were battling blazes at the St Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchi oil depot and industrial warehouses in the Kolpino district south of the city.
The governor said several residential buildings were also hit, along with two houses.
City authorities said the attack disrupted flights at St Petersburg’s main airport, one of the country’s busiest, which was restricting operations “for safety reasons”, Beglov said.
Russian e-commerce company Ozon said there was a fire at its logistics hub in St Petersburg, and the internet company VK said its data centre in the Leningrad region had been attacked by drones, adding that normal services were available to users.
The governor of the Leningrad region surrounding St Petersburg, Alexander Drozdenko, said 145 drones had been shot down and about 20,000 people were without electricity following the drone raid.
Russia’s state-run news agency TASS said the attack was the largest on the region in the last four years.
Moscow’s defence ministry said 1,015 Ukrainian drones were neutralised overnight.
Russian strikes kill two
In Ukraine, Russian forces struck residential buildings overnight, killing two people and injuring 12, including two children, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X on Sunday.
“This morning, there was a strike on an agricultural enterprise in Volyn. All necessary services are working at the site,” he said.
“In total, over this past week, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic.”
The attacks came after Zelenskyy said this week that Kyiv would resume hitting Russian refineries, insisting he was standing up for his war-torn country, as support from the United States declined.
Zelenskyy told the British newspaper the Financial Times this week that Kyiv was “done” with an “energy ceasefire” unilaterally declared by United States President Donald Trump and would resume strikes on Russia in retaliation for a wave of attacks.
‘Energy ceasefire’ falters
Trump announced an immediate “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine last week, but Zelenskyy said Moscow continued to violate the deal.
“Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ago, Russia has deliberately attacked Ukraine’s energy and oil and gas sectors 76 times,” he wrote in his X post on Sunday.
“Last night alone, there were strikes on substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions,” he wrote, adding that tens of thousands of families remained without power as energy workers and repair crews worked round the clock to restore supplies.
Zelenskyy also said that the main targets of Moscow’s recent strikes were energy facilities, as the Russians were trying to “cause a blackout”.
“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” he said.
Trump is also facing criticism in both Europe and the US after he signed an executive order on Friday to waive sanctions and tariffs targeting Moscow’s energy revenues.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that Trump’s waiver would be a pause to “analyse” their impact on the global economy.
“The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia.
Trump said late on Saturday his decision would benefit the US.
“We’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” he said. “It’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world.”

articles.title: Zelenskyy warns US’ Russia sanctions relief could reward Putin and fuel more attacks
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that US President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russia could encourage the Kremlin to continue its war against Ukraine, saying he fears further concessions to Moscow.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving sweeping US sanctions targeting Russian energy revenues, prompting concern in Kiev as Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure continue.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said he feared the move was only the beginning of a broader relaxation of restrictions.
“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the ‘diesel deal’ is just the first step,” Zelenskyy told reporters.
He said he still personally hoped Trump would do everything in his power to persuade Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war, but argued that limiting Ukraine’s ability to respond to Russian attacks while easing pressure on Moscow would not achieve that goal.
At least two people were reported killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine on Saturday, according to Ukrainian officials.
Russian strikes hit Ukraine’s energy infrastructure
Zelenskyy said the US sanctions decision came on the same day Russia attacked 15 critical power-generation facilities across Ukraine in what he described as one of the largest assaults on the country’s energy grid.
Officials said a Russian attack in the southern city of Kherson killed one person and wounded 22 others, including two children. Another person was killed in the northeastern city of Sumy.
Zelenskyy warned that Russia was seeking to leave millions of Ukrainians without electricity and heating ahead of winter, when damage to energy infrastructure could have severe consequences for civilians.
Last winter, hundreds of thousands of people in Ukraine experienced prolonged interruptions to heating and electricity during freezing temperatures.
The Ukrainian president called on Kiev’s allies to increase pressure on Moscow and argued that sanctions were intended to raise the cost of continuing the war.
Kiev urges Washington to maintain pressure on Moscow
Zelenskyy also appealed to the United States to reconsider its approach to sanctions, highlighting the Lindsey Graham Act, which targets Russia’s energy and defence sectors, Putin and the so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western restrictions.
The legislation, named after the late US senator who sponsored it, was intended to increase economic pressure on Moscow.
“It is important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening,” Zelenskyy said on social media, arguing that the sanctions framework could still help bring the conflict to an end.
He warned that easing restrictions while Russia continued attacking Ukraine risked rewarding the aggressor and encouraging further military action.
Trump’s sanctions waiver followed his announcement of a deal with Putin allowing Russian diesel exports in exchange for sanctions relief.
The US president’s move came shortly after Putin, appearing in military uniform, said Moscow aimed to capture the remaining parts of eastern Ukraine.
Moscow welcomes Trump’s decision as talks stall
Russian officials welcomed the sanctions relief, although the Kremlin and Putin had not issued a direct response to Trump’s announcement at the time of the report.
Kirill Dmitriev, a Putin envoy, described the suspension of the Graham Act as an “important and truly historic moment”. He argued that the legislation would have caused serious damage to the US economy and global markets.
Zelenskyy met European leaders in Brussels on Friday, urging the European Union to continue financing Ukraine’s defence. He said he was standing up for his country amid the dispute with Washington.
As Russian strikes continue and winter approaches, Kiev is pressing its allies to sustain economic and military support while diplomatic efforts to end the conflict remain uncertain.

articles.title: US Congress Stalled on Response to Trump Russia Waiver – AP
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump’s decision to indefinitely postpone statutory sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia has triggered condemnation from lawmakers across both parties, though formal congressional intervention remains stalled due to the pre-election legislative recess, the Associated Press reported.
Congress previously passed the sanctions package with overwhelming veto-proof majorities, reflecting broad bipartisan backing for Ukraine and international deterrence.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
However, Trump’s executive order on Friday, Oct. 16, waiving enforcement just 48 hours before statutory enactment ignited pushback among key Republican and Democratic legislators.
Despite the outrage, lawmakers are not positioned to mount an immediate legislative response, as both the Senate and the House of Representatives remain in recess until after the crucial Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Republican fury and challenges to energy rationale
Senior Republicans voiced open frustration over the administration’s decision to shield Moscow from statutory trade duties and secondary financial penalties.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis characterized the executive waiver as “more than irresponsible,” pointing out that the Senate enacted the statute by an overwhelming 86-11 margin. Tillis accused the White House of offering unwarranted concessions to Russian President Vladimir Putin while undermining congressional prerogatives.
Tillis further pushed back against the administration’s economic defense, stating that if the White House seeks to reduce domestic energy prices, policymakers must focus on resolving the armed conflict involving Iran rather than enacting commercial steps that subsidize Russia.
Zelensky Calls Trump’s Sanctions Waiver a Mistake
Democratic leadership pledges congressional pushback
Democratic leaders similarly condemned the indefinite suspension, warning that easing economic pressure underwrites the Kremlin’s wartime economy and sustains long-range bombardments against Ukrainian civilian population centers.
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer accused Trump of directly propping up the Russian economy at the expense of American allies and democratic norms.
Senator Elizabeth Warren stated that the president is openly defying Congress, asserting that waiving statutory enforcement enables Putin to prolong an aggressive war of conquest.
Warren urged lawmakers to prepare legislative mechanisms to reverse the executive order once Congress reconvenes in Washington following the November vote.
The Associated Press reported that Trump suspended the penalties indefinitely, citing US national security considerations under statutory waiver authorities.
Because members of Congress are dispersed across their home districts campaigning ahead of the Nov. 3 balloting, any formal legislative counter-measures – such as the bipartisan “Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act” introduced by Representative Gregory Meeks or the “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act” drafted by Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick and Don Bacon – will face procedural delays until post-election sessions commence.
Background on the Graham Act and the diesel deal
Trump’s executive action waives core enforcement mechanisms codified within the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which the president signed into law on Sept. 18.
The suspended provisions, which were scheduled to take statutory effect on Sunday, Oct. 18, mandated an additional 500 percent tariff on all Russian-origin imports alongside 100 percent duties targeting the five largest global purchasers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, including China and India.
The statute also required trade penalties against third-party nations facilitating petroleum sanctions evasion and established aggressive actions to dismantle Moscow’s maritime “shadow fleet.”
In issuing the waiver, Trump invoked Section 115 of the statute, which grants executive discretion upon certifying to Congress that such action serves US national interests.
The suspension aligns with a commercial arrangement unveiled on Oct. 9 between Trump and Putin, under which Moscow consented to export refined diesel onto international markets through 2027 to lower retail fuel costs.
The waiver was met with condemnation from Kyiv, where President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that lifting economic penalties constitutes a grave policy error that provides financial lifelines to the Russian military and signals to Moscow that persistent infrastructure bombardments will carry no economic consequence.

articles.title: Blunder in, abandon allies and court a dictator: it’s the Trump doctrine, now playing out in Myanmar | Steve Bloomfield
articles.body:
Marco Rubio was once adamant that the US had to do everything in its power to end what he described as the “ethnic cleansing” of the Rohingya in Myanmar. In a 2017 letter he signed along with 20 other US senators, Rubio called for “strong multilateral sanctions against specific senior Burmese military officials associated with the gross human rights abuses”. Those responsible for the atrocities should be prosecuted, he argued.
In the years since, the Myanmar military’s crimes have only increased. What was then deemed ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya is now widely viewed, including by the US, as genocide. What little democracy existed in Myanmar was eradicated in 2021 when Aung San Suu Kyi was arrested and imprisoned and her party’s election victory overturned, and the military took full control.
This sparked a civil war that has now turned into a brutal series of overlapping conflicts between the military, resistance forces and a medley of ethnic militias. Around 100,000 people have been killed in the conflict, which has forced 5 million people to flee their homes. The UN estimates that 16 million are now in need of urgent assistance. It is one of the world’s biggest humanitarian disasters – and entirely human-made.
Earlier this year, Myanmar held sham elections, and Min Aung Hlaing – the general most responsible for Myanmar’s genocide and one of the targets of Rubio’s letter – became president.
But Rubio, now the US secretary of state, no longer believes that Min Aung Hlaing should be prosecuted. Instead he’d rather like him to become an ally. This month the Trump administration decided to upend nearly a decade of united western policy and open direct talks with the Myanmar regime. The possibility of lifting sanctions is now being discussed. The move has shocked other western nations – none of which, it appears, was warned.
Inevitably, a Maga figure lingers in the background. This time it’s Roger Stone, the Donald Trump ally who was found guilty in 2019 of lying to Congress, witness tampering and obstructing the investigation into whether the Trump campaign conspired with Russia in the 2016 presidential election.
Stone, who was spared jail after Trump commuted his sentence, recently started working as a lobbyist for the Myanmar regime, helping to “rebuild relations between the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and the United States”.
It seems to be working. Earlier this month Michael Vance, the assistant secretary of state for intelligence and research, travelled to Myanmar’s capital Naypyidaw. The trip was supposedly to secure the release of a US citizen, but Vance also held talks with the generals. The purpose of the talks was not to persuade the military regime to reintroduce democracy or stop its brutal war. Instead it appeared to be about securing American access to Myanmar’s rare earth minerals.
In recent years, the race to control a steady supply of rare-earth minerals – elements used in a host of military technology and hi-tech manufacturing applications – has become increasingly fraught. China controls most of the world’s rare-earth mines and almost all of the processing capacity. The Trump administration’s desire to turn the tables has led it to strike one-sided deals with Ukraine and the Democratic Republic of Congo that have placed US business interests over practically everything else.
There are more than 600 rare earth mines in Myanmar, most of which currently supply China. Since the 2021 coup, rare-earth shipments from Myanmar to China have totalled $3.6bn, making up the majority of China’s rare-earth imports. This is the prize the US appears to have its eyes on.
Vance’s trip has handed Myanmar’s generals a propaganda victory at a moment when they are doing everything they can to legitimise the regime. The US, unfortunately, is not the only country welcoming Myanmar’s generals back into the fold. Min Aung Hlaing this month flew to Malaysia, once a strong opponent of the junta, where the prime minister Anwar Imbrahim floated the idea of Myanmar being welcomed back into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean). Trips to Indonesia and Brunei are also on the cards, while the Philippines has indicated that it too would like to see relations normalised.
The junta’s diplomatic victories follow growing military success. Over the last two and a half years, with the help of more sophisticated drones supplied by Russia and China, and the conscription of another 100,000 young men, the junta has regained control over several towns and pushed the resistance back into the countryside.
For Myanmar’s civilians, the long nightmare continues. Last month more than 50 people were killed when the military bombed a busy market in a rebel-held area. Every week brings fresh atrocities, while the hope of a peaceful, democratic Myanmar slips further into the distance.
The one silver lining that those fighting for Myanmar’s freedom can cling to is that the rest of the west hasn’t given up on it yet. British diplomats are adamant that there will be no change in the UK’s position, while Canada, Australia and the EU are all likely to hold the line too. But even here there are concerns.
Campaigners point to the UK’s recent reduction in aid to Myanmar from £66m a year to £55m. Just half of the $889.6m the UN has requested for Myanmar this year has been provided by international donors. They would also like to see Britain and others engage more directly with Myanmar’s pro-democracy camp, including the resistance.
Trump is not the first president to prioritise resources over democracy, as a cursory glance at US relations with Saudi Arabia since it discovered oil in 1938 shows. But Trump’s rapacious attitude to oil and minerals, his willingness to enrich his friends and family, and his brazen support for dictators makes this a very different America. Myanmar is simply another example of the corrosive nature that Trump’s foreign policy is having in every corner of the globe.
The question is whether Trump will get what he wants. US policy on Myanmar has been driven by Congress, and there remains bipartisan support for keeping it in place. The House of Representatives recently passed a bill that would extend the sanctions regime for another six years. Particularly at a time when his support is waning, Trump is unlikely to have much joy in persuading senators and members of Congress who have long supported Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement to turn a blind eye to genocide and war crimes.
Even if he did, the bigger question is whether Myanmar’s generals can give Trump what he wants. The vast majority of Myanmar’s rare earth mines are near the border with China and many are controlled by militia groups, not the junta. “There is no way China is going to let the US get anywhere near the rare earths,” Joshua Kurlantzick at the Council on Foreign Relations told me.
And yet even if none of this leads to any real change, the Trump administration’s decision to open talks with a genocidal regime responsible for one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises is a disaster for those in Myanmar fighting for their freedom. Many Myanmar resistance figures, including Aung San Suu Kyi, have placed their hope in US help. Like other democrats fighting demagogues, such as Volodymyr Zelenskyy, they have been deserted.
Here is yet another example of the Trump administration blundering into a part of the world where it knows little, offering a prize to an authoritarian and leaving with not much to show for it.
- Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

articles.title: Trump yet to give final decision on Russia tariffs, sanctions, as Rubio says more time needed
articles.body:
The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter, as Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation.
Rubio said on Saturday that the president will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlier.
"A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida.
The waiver comes just weeks before November's midterm elections, with Trump under pressure over high energy prices as war with Iran disrupts global oil supplies.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham Act, which he signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next week. Friday's order didn't specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump chose a 60-day review.
"I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan.
Complicating matters is the Graham Act's call not only for sanctions on Russia but also for tariffs on goods from countries that import Russian energy supplies. Rubio pointed to India, an important US partner that has diversified its energy supplies but remains heavily dependent on Russian oil.
Trump's decision draws criticism from Zelensky, Republican senator
Friday's executive order drew criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who warned it would embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war.
Senator Darline Graham, a South Carolina Republican whose late brother Lindsey Graham championed the legislation that bears his name, said she disagreed with Trump's decision and planned to discuss it with him when he campaigns for her next week.
"Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia," she told reporters on Saturday. "Because I don't trust Putin and I don't trust Russia."
Rubio also defended a separate US agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies.
Under the agreement, Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States, followed by shipments in November and beyond.
"That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get."
Rubio said the diesel deal and sanctions waiver reflected the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies.
"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," he said.

articles.title: Zelensky criticises Trump’s waiver of sanctions on Russia as ‘wrong’
articles.body:
Zelensky criticises Trump’s waiver of sanctions on Russia as ‘wrong’
- Donald Trump waived planned US sanctions and tariffs on Russia, saying it was in America’s national interest. Volodymyr Zelensky called the move “wrong” and said it only helps Russia.
- Zelensky warned the decision will embolden Vladimir Putin and lead to more attacks on Ukraine. He said Russia hit more than 15 power sites and may target western Ukraine next.
- Russia praised the waiver as “a truly historic moment”. US critics said Trump was giving in to Putin, while the Graham Act could still be used to restore pressure later.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect, will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct 17, predicting even more US sanctions relief.
“The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me,” Zelensky wrote on X. “It definitely helps only the Russians.”
An executive order issued by Trump on the night of Oct 16 waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs – including duties on the country’s goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas – that had been scheduled to start next week under the legislation known as the Graham Act that he signed into law in September.
Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the US.
The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming towards Moscow while publicly criticising Zelensky, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.
Zelensky said the latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people,” wrote Zelensky, who said Russia struck more than 15 Ukrainian power generation and transmission sites on Oct 16. “This certainly does not stop the war.”
He accused Russia of planning to ramp up strikes in western Ukraine. “Is Russia preparing for this? I think so,” Zelensky wrote.
Russian envoy praises waiver
Russia’s investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, called the Trump waiver “a truly historic moment”, posting on X on Oct 16 that had the penalties taken effect, they could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a halt.
Weeks before US midterm elections in which Trump’s Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked further raising oil prices as Americans face increased costs largely due to the US-Israeli war with Iran, analysts said.
Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.
The legislation’s primary backer in Congress was the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican. It would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.
Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to fill his Senate seat after he died in July, and Trump endorsed her for a full term heading into the midterm elections. At a campaign stop on Oct 17, she did not directly criticise Trump for waiving sanctions, but said she would not have made that choice.
“Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia,” she told reporters, according to multiple news outlets. “Because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia.”
China and India, which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, had raised concerns about the Graham Act.
Beijing said it “consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law”, while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties.
But the Graham Act also allows the president to waive sanctions by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest. The Oct 16 executive order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that “further action is appropriate”.
US Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said Trump was giving in to Putin.
“Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression,” Beyer said in a statement on Oct 16.
Lindsey Graham, who died in July, strongly supported US assistance to Ukraine. The passage of the bill named for him had provided hope of continued bipartisan support for Kyiv, wrote Zelensky.
But with Graham gone, the US under Trump will continue sanctions relief for Russia beyond the Oct 16 waiver and the diesel export agreement announced earlier in October, the Ukrainian leader predicted.
“I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately,” wrote Zelensky, who lamented Graham’s absence. “It’s unfortunate because we all had great respect for Lindsey... It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest.” REUTERS

articles.title: Ukraine runs out of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles as Trump snubs Zelensky - report
articles.body:
Ukraine has run out of missiles for the US-made Patriot air defense system, a source familiar with the situation told CNN on Thursday.
This development comes amid a series of public jabs between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky.
Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, Zelensky said on Saturday, predicting even more US sanctions relief.
"The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelensky wrote on X. "It definitely helps only the Russians."
An executive order issued by Trump on Friday night waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs, including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas, that were scheduled to take effect next week under the Graham Act, which he signed into law last month.
Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the United States.
The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming toward Moscow while publicly criticizing Zelensky, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.
Zelensky hopes for meeting with US and Russia during G20 summit
Ukraine, the United States and Russia could meet during a G20 summit in the US, but Washington and Moscow have not confirmed the meeting and other venues are also possible, Zelensky said on Saturday.
The Group of 20 major economies, which includes the US and Russia but not Ukraine, is due to hold a summit in Miami in December.
"The meeting could then take place in the United States during the G20 summit. But there has been no confirmation yet from either Russia or the United States. It could also be held in a European country," Zelensky told reporters in a WhatsApp media chat.
Ukraine says unable to use interceptors due to Starlink limits, in touch with US
This comes as Starlink disruptions are being felt on the front lines of the war in Ukraine.
Ukraine cannot use its interceptor systems against Russian drone attacks because of speed restrictions imposed on Starlink, Zelensky said on Saturday, adding that Kyiv was discussing the issue with US officials.
Zelensky told reporters in a WhatsApp media chat that Ukrainian officials had been told the restrictions were linked to technical issues.
He said Ukraine had tested Starlink on European Union territory and encountered no such problems there, with the system operating at higher speeds.

articles.title: British startup develos modular ground drone for front line
articles.body:
- UK-based Stratonex Defence Technologies unveiled VARAN, a modular unmanned ground vehicle concept for ISR, logistics, force protection, electronic warfare and counter-drone missions.
- The company says VARAN can navigate without GPS, uses passive 3D sensing and is designed for low visual, thermal and acoustic signatures.
British defense technology company Stratonex Defence Technologies has unveiled VARAN, a modular unmanned ground vehicle concept designed to accompany and support forward units on the battlefield, with swappable mission equipment and the ability to navigate without satellite positioning.
The company introduced the vehicle on social media and on its website, describing VARAN as a payload-agnostic platform that can be configured for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, logistics, force protection, electronic warfare and counter-drone missions.
Stratonex says VARAN uses autonomous navigation and passive 3D sensing to move across rough terrain, including in areas where GPS and other satellite navigation signals are jammed or unavailable. Passive sensing means the vehicle builds a picture of its surroundings without emitting signals such as radar or lidar pulses that an enemy could detect, and the company says the platform is designed to keep a low visual, thermal and acoustic signature.
The vehicle is built on an open systems architecture, which Stratonex says allows mission-specific payloads and future technologies to be integrated as requirements change. The company pitches VARAN as a way for troops to move farther and carry more in expeditionary operations, from reconnaissance support to counter-drone and rapid deployment tasks.
Stratonex framed the platform around configuration and integration, asking what capabilities potential users would want added to an unmanned ground vehicle.
Stratonex is a UK-based company co-founded by Ben Everitt, a former Conservative member of Parliament for Milton Keynes North, and describes itself as a developer of autonomous systems and mission software focused on sovereign capability for Britain and its allies. In July 2026, Nasdaq-listed VisionWave Holdings appointed Stratonex as its commercialization and integration partner for the UK and Europe under a non-exclusive distributor agreement covering VisionWave’s autonomous systems, sensing and counter-drone technologies.
Uncrewed ground vehicles have become a growing focus for European armies after their wide use in the war in Ukraine, where both sides rely on them to haul supplies, evacuate wounded troops and carry weapons along front lines exposed to constant drone surveillance. Britain’s Ministry of Defence has also been funding and trialing uncrewed ground platforms for logistics and combat support roles.
Stratonex presents VARAN as a concept platform, and the company is inviting feedback from potential users on which capabilities to integrate as development continues.

articles.title: Romania shoots down two drones over Black Sea
articles.body:
Romania has said it shot down two drones that entered its airspace over the Black Sea, the latest in a series of incidents believed to be spillover from Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Facebook on Saturday that Romanian F-16 fighter jets intercepted and shot down both drones about 20 kilometres southeast of Sulina.
“Two drones were engaged and shot down a few minutes ago by Romanian military pilots over the Black Sea, moments after they had illegally entered our country,” he wrote.
The first drone entered Romanian airspace at 17:59 local time (14:59 GMT) and was shot down within two minutes, Miruta said.
The second was downed at 18:05, five minutes after crossing into the country’s airspace.
Two F-16 fighter jets of the Romanian Air Force engaged the drones, according to a press release of the defence ministry.
NATO has previously shot down four drones in Romania's airspace, all of them this year.
Russian drone incursions
Romania, a NATO member bordering Ukraine, has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions since the Russia-Ukraine war began in February 2022. Much of the border follows the Danube, close to Ukrainian ports targeted by Russian forces.
The latest incident follows drone strikes on two tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast earlier this week.
Romanian authorities resumed searches on Friday for seven missing sailors from one of the vessels, raising further concerns about the war’s impact on commercial shipping.
Neighbouring Bulgaria has also requested NATO combat aircraft and anti-drone systems following attacks on ships in the Black Sea. Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Friday that Sofia had formally sought additional support to strengthen its defences.

articles.title: Ukrainian Officials Slam Trump's Waiver Of Russia Sanctions As Rubio Defends Move
articles.body:
Ukrainian officials sharply criticized US President Donald Trump's decision to waive sweeping planned sanctions against Russia, saying that it "sends the wrong message to the aggressor" and "helps only the Russians."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration needed up to 60 days to assess the potential economic impact of the sanctions and tariffs, while the White House argued that imposing them immediately could hinder efforts to negotiate a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine.
"If Russians are cheering yesterday's decisions in the US, it is certainly not about effective pressure to end the war," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha wrote on X on October 17. "Indecisiveness sends the wrong signal to the aggressor. It only prolongs the war."
He added that "Lindsey Graham understood this well," referring to the late senator of South Carolina for whom the sanctions legislation, known as the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 -- was named. Graham, who died on July 11, was a prominent congressional supporter of Ukraine.
The bill passed Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and was signed into law by Trump in September. But in an executive order signed late on October 16, Trump said withholding the measures was in the national interest of the United States. The order came just two days before the sanctions package was due to take effect on October 18.
The move prompted sharp criticism from Ukraine advocates and lawmakers from both parties who say the move undermines efforts to force Moscow to negotiate.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said removing the sanctions "definitely helps only the Russians."
"The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskiy wrote on X on October 17.
The law was designed to give the administration additional leverage over Russian President Vladimir Putin by authorizing tariffs of up to 100 percent on major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India, and providing for sanctions targeting Russian officials, financial institutions, and the country's so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent existing restrictions.
Rubio defended the White House's decision to waive new sanctions on Russia on October 17, saying Washington needed time to assess the economic consequences of additional penalties as conflicts across several regions strain global energy supplies.
Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews before departing for a series of diplomatic and trade talks in Central Asia, Rubio defended the administration's efforts to balance pressure on Moscow against economic concerns.
The waiver followed a diesel deal Trump announced with Russia on October 9 that prompted criticism that Washington was prioritizing domestic fuel prices over efforts to constrain the Kremlin's war against Ukraine.
Zelenskyy called the waiver was an unfortunate decision to backtrack on the sanctions at a time when "pressure is needed."
"At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote on X.
"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine -- right before winter," he said. "Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating. Pressure is needed to stop this. A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin -- all of this only encourages him to keep attacking."
A senior envoy to Russian President Vladimir Putin, meanwhile, praised the waiver as "a truly historic moment."
Kirill Dmitriev, who heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, wrote on X late on October 16 that "economic cooperation between Russia and the United States serves the interest of both nations."
Energy Costs Complicate Russia Sanctions
Rubio said the administration needed 60 days to assess the effects of sanctions and tariffs, including their potential impact on countries such as India, which continues to rely substantially on Russian energy despite efforts to diversify its supplies.
He pointed to disruptions involving Iran, the Strait of Hormuz, attacks by Yemen's Houthi movement, and the war between Russia and Ukraine as factors putting pressure on global energy markets.
"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," Rubio said.
The United States was paying higher prices than it wanted, he said, while some other countries were approaching a crisis over energy costs and availability.
Rubio also defended the administration's diesel deal with Russia -- which Zelenskyy called "a gift" to Putin -- arguing the fuel would have reached international markets regardless of whether the United States purchased it. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get," he said.
Energy analysts have questioned whether the deal would significantly lower prices for American consumers, while warning that easing restrictions could provide Moscow with substantial economic benefits.
The waiver blocks additional sanctions and tariffs approved by Congress to discourage major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, although existing sanctions remain in place.
The decision drew sharp criticism from both parties.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible," while Senator John Cornyn said the late senator Graham "would be appalled." Democratic lawmakers also accused Trump of helping Russia finance its war.
