articles.title: Russia’s war in Ukraine puts Europe on edge
articles.body:
Talk to Al Jazeera
Russia’s war in Ukraine puts Europe on edge
Fears are growing that Russia’s war in Ukraine could spill over into neighbouring NATO members – and spread regionally.
Some countries would argue it already has – pointing to drone incursions, cyberattacks and sabotage.
European nations say Moscow is targeting Ukraine’s allies to intimidate them. The Kremlin denies the accusations.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warns Europe should be ready to respond robustly to Russia’s hybrid attacks.
Poland, which borders Ukraine, is home to a NATO logistics hub used for military and civilian support to its neighbour.
The International Centre for Counterterrorism says the country is the ‘primary focus’ of Russia’s sabotage campaign in Europe.
It’s also the country most targeted by cyberattacks, according to research from Harvard, with about four thousand politically motivated attacks per day.
And Poland is on heightened alert.
It’s reported several airspace violations — and authorities say more drone and missile strikes are likely.
Sikorski says that for the war to end Russian President Vladimir Putin would have to admit his original goals are unachievable and that the full-scale invasion of Ukraine was a mistake.

articles.title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,565,060 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
articles.body:
Russia has lost 1,565,060 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 18.
The number includes 2,090 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,416 tanks, 25,561 armored combat vehicles, 164,246 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,293 artillery systems, 2,224 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,711 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,968 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Newest TOS-3 Dragon Thermobaric Rocket Launcher for First Time, Video
articles.body:

Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Newest TOS-3 Dragon Thermobaric Rocket Launcher for First Time, Video
Ukrainian forces have struck Russia’s newest TOS-3 “Dragon” heavy flamethrower system for the first time, using a drone to target the tracked thermobaric rocket launcher approximately 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) behind the front line.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s Third Army Corps on October 17, the strike was carried out by operators of the Muramasa unit, part of the Kraken Unmanned Systems Regiment, during the ongoing offensive operation known as “Vivaldi.”
The Ukrainian military said the Russian launcher was identified after it had conducted a firing mission. Drone operators subsequently located and struck the system, with footage of the engagement released through the corps’ official channels.
The Third Army Corps described the attack as the first reported successful strike against the TOS-3, a recently developed Russian weapon designed to deliver thermobaric rockets against fortified positions and concentrations of troops.
The TOS-3 “Dragon” is the latest addition to Russia’s family of heavy flamethrower systems, following the TOS-1A “Solntsepyok” and TOS-2 “Tosochka.”
Unlike the wheeled TOS-2, the TOS-3 uses a tracked, tank-type chassis intended to improve mobility across difficult terrain while providing greater protection for its crew.
According to specifications shared by the Third Army Corps, the launcher carries 15 tubes for unguided thermobaric rockets and has an estimated firing range of up to 15 kilometers (9.3 miles).
The system is operated by a three-person crew and incorporates additional protective measures, including slat armor and explosive reactive armor intended to improve its survivability against incoming attacks.
Thermobaric weapons use explosive mixtures that generate intense heat and prolonged blast pressure, making them particularly destructive against enclosed positions, trenches, and fortified structures.
The reported strike took place during Operation Vivaldi, an offensive campaign conducted by Ukraine’s Third Army Corps in the northern part of the Donetsk region.
During the same operation, Ukrainian forces deployed unmanned ground vehicles behind Russian positions, contributing to the liberation of two villages and the clearing of another settlement.
Ukrainian units also adapted ground-based attack drones with grenade launchers to engage Russian positions, demonstrating the expanding use of unmanned systems in offensive operations.

articles.title: Trump waves Russia sanctions passed by Congress amid deepening row with Ukraine
articles.body:
Trump waves Russia sanctions passed by Congress amid deepening row with Ukraine
Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest, the Guardian reported.
In an executive order on Friday, the president said he was waiving many sanctions, restrictions and duties on Russia, in a move that comes as he has been publicly criticizing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including suggesting that Ukraine needs a new leader.
The move was greeted by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote on social media: “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment.”
Trump signed the legislation last month, after Congress passed the measure in an act of rare bipartisan agreement. It sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia’s war in Ukraine.
The legislation – whose primary backer in Congress was the late senator Lindsey Graham – sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving and was due to be implemented in two days.
It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Friday’s announcement comes a week after Trump said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of U.S. and Western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.
Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1m tons “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
Under the legislation he signed into law, Trump had until October 18 to impose the sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy, or waive them. The administration had not told lawmakers whether it would impose the sanctions or issue a waiver.
Facing midterm elections on November 3, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that could cost his Republican party its thin majorities in the US Senate and House of Representatives.

articles.title: Trump calls decision to waive sanctions against Russia "very good" for US and "the world"

articles.title: Iran urges US to accept proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday.
Iran presented its proposal in mid-September after an interim ceasefire collapsed. Tehran later acknowledged receiving a US response, but Iran’s security chief said last week negotiations have stalled because Washington failed to address all seven conditions for reopening the strait.
"Our situation is clear and based on the seven-days proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn't, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious," Araqchi said while in Baghdad for a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis on Sunday said two pilots were killed when their helicopter crashed because of a "technical malfunction" near the border with Yemen, the first military fatalities since hostilities restarted in July.
The British navy-affiliated UKMTO said on Sunday it received a report of an incident northeast of Khor Fakkan in the United Arab Emirates, where a tug sailing southbound was struck by two unknown projectiles.
One minor injury was reported, and the tug sustained damage; however, UKMTO added that it is continuing on its route.
Police said Saturday a social media post by the wife of the British prime minister's national security advisor backing banned activist group Palestine Action did not merit a criminal investigation.
Sarah Helm, a journalist and author and wife of Jonathan Powell, Prime Minister Andy Burnham's national security adviser, posted on X Thursday "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action", an activist group banned as terrorist by the UK government last year.
A spokesperson for the capital's police force said Saturday specialist officers had looked at the post and ruled it "did not meet the criminal threshold" and "no further police action will be taken".
Riyadh's Kingdom Centre skyscraper, one of the city's major landmarks, ordered its office tenants to work remotely "until further notice" on Sunday, after repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
"Kindly refrain from attending the offices during this period," the office management said in an email to tenants seen by AFP. The mall at the foot of the 99-storey building remains open.
Iran urges US to accept proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday.
If Washington accepts Tehran's conditions, the strategic waterway would be open within six days, and US-Iran talks would resume on the seventh day, he added.
Egypt: Will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary support
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee sharply condemned settler violence during an olive harvest in the West Bank that injured several Palestinians and Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine as “a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards.” In a post late Saturday on X, he called for “a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this.”
Levine was seriously injured in the attack Friday in the West Bank village of Abu Falah. Israeli police are also investigating an attack by Israeli settlers on European diplomats Saturday in another West Bank village. Settler violence against Palestinians has soared this year and spiked further in recent weeks as Israel plans to hold elections on 27 October.
Iranian lawmakers on Sunday approved Mehrdad Akhlaghi as the country's new defence minister, replacing his predecessor, who was killed on the first day of the war with the United States.
"Members of the Islamic Consultative Assembly today gave vote of confidence to Mehrdad Akhlaghi, the nominee for minister of defence and armed forces logistics," state television reported, nearly eight months after the initial US-Israeli strikes that sparked the conflict.
Saudi-led coalition: Two pilots killed in helicopter crash
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis on Sunday said two pilots were killed when their helicopter crashed because of a "technical malfunction" near the border with Yemen, the first military fatalities since hostilities restarted in July.
"An AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter belonging to the national guard crashed and was destroyed in Saudi territory in the Najran area as a result of a technical malfunction, resulting in the death of its crew of two officers," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said, according to the official Saudi Press Agency.
After a four-year, uneasy truce, Yemen's conflict reignited in July and intensified when the Iran-backed group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
Tug off UAE's Khor Fakkan struck by two projectiles
The British navy-affiliated UKMTO said on Sunday that it has received a report of an incident northeast of Khor Fakkan in the United Arab Emirates, where a tug sailing southbound reported being struck by two unknown projectiles.
One minor injury was reported and the tug has sustained damage, however is continuing on its route, UKMTO added.

Ukraine Hits Russia’s Railway Bridge in Bryansk, Blasts Military Supply Depots Across Donetsk
Ukrainian forces struck a railway bridge in Russia’s Bryansk region and several Russian military logistics facilities in temporarily occupied Donetsk region during operations conducted on October 16 and overnight into October 17.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on October 17, the strikes targeted infrastructure used by Russian forces to transport military supplies, store equipment, and coordinate drone operations.
One of the targets was a railway bridge spanning the Unecha River near Sloboda-Seletskaya in Russia’s Bryansk region. Ukrainian military officials confirmed that the bridge had been hit but did not specify the extent of the damage.
The railway crossing is part of the transport infrastructure that can be used to move military cargo. Disrupting such routes could complicate Russian efforts to deliver ammunition, fuel, and military equipment to its forces operating in Ukraine.
Separately, Ukrainian forces struck Russian military supply depots in three locations across temporarily occupied Donetsk region.
The General Staff identified the areas near Novoandriivka, Nikolske, and Mariupol as the locations of the attacks. The facilities were reportedly used to store logistical supplies supporting Russian military operations.
Another strike targeted a Russian unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) command post near Malynivka in Donetsk region. The Ukrainian military did not disclose the type of weapons used or provide an assessment of Russian equipment losses.
Earlier, on October 16, Ukrainian forces targeted a second Russian Mi-28NM attack helicopter in less than a week using a domestically produced VB140 Flamingo interceptor drone over Russia’s Belgorod region. Footage released by Ukraine’s 115th Separate Mechanized Brigade showed the drone approaching the helicopter, although the extent of any damage remains unconfirmed.

Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday.
Iran presented its proposal in mid-September after an interim ceasefire collapsed. Tehran later acknowledged receiving a US response, but Iran’s security chief said last week negotiations have stalled because Washington failed to address all seven conditions for reopening the strait.
"Our situation is clear and based on the seven-days proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn't, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious," Araqchi said while in Baghdad for a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis on Sunday said two pilots were killed when their helicopter crashed because of a "technical malfunction" near the border with Yemen, the first military fatalities since hostilities restarted in July.
The British navy-affiliated UKMTO said on Sunday it received a report of an incident northeast of Khor Fakkan in the United Arab Emirates, where a tug sailing southbound was struck by two unknown projectiles.
One minor injury was reported, and the tug sustained damage; however, UKMTO added that it is continuing on its route.
Police said Saturday a social media post by the wife of the British prime minister's national security advisor backing banned activist group Palestine Action did not merit a criminal investigation.
Sarah Helm, a journalist and author and wife of Jonathan Powell, Prime Minister Andy Burnham's national security adviser, posted on X Thursday "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action", an activist group banned as terrorist by the UK government last year.
A spokesperson for the capital's police force said Saturday specialist officers had looked at the post and ruled it "did not meet the criminal threshold" and "no further police action will be taken".
Riyadh's Kingdom Centre skyscraper, one of the city's major landmarks, ordered its office tenants to work remotely "until further notice" on Sunday, after repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
"Kindly refrain from attending the offices during this period," the office management said in an email to tenants seen by AFP. The mall at the foot of the 99-storey building remains open.
Iran urges US to accept proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday.
If Washington accepts Tehran's conditions, the strategic waterway would be open within six days, and US-Iran talks would resume on the seventh day, he added.
Egypt: Will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary support
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee sharply condemned settler violence during an olive harvest in the West Bank that injured several Palestinians and Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine as “a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards.” In a post late Saturday on X, he called for “a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this.”
Levine was seriously injured in the attack Friday in the West Bank village of Abu Falah. Israeli police are also investigating an attack by Israeli settlers on European diplomats Saturday in another West Bank village. Settler violence against Palestinians has soared this year and spiked further in recent weeks as Israel plans to hold elections on 27 October.
Iranian lawmakers on Sunday approved Mehrdad Akhlaghi as the country's new defence minister, replacing his predecessor, who was killed on the first day of the war with the United States.
"Members of the Islamic Consultative Assembly today gave vote of confidence to Mehrdad Akhlaghi, the nominee for minister of defence and armed forces logistics," state television reported, nearly eight months after the initial US-Israeli strikes that sparked the conflict.

"An AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter belonging to the national guard crashed and was destroyed in Saudi territory in the Najran area as a result of a technical malfunction, resulting in the death of its crew of two officers," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said, according to the official Saudi Press Agency.
After a four-year, uneasy truce, Yemen's conflict reignited in July and intensified when the Iran-backed group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.

articles.title: Iran's FM says Tehran ready for dialogue based on mutual respect, credible guarantees
articles.body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that his country will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure, but remains "ready for dialogue based on mutual respect and credible guarantees."
Araghchi made the remarks at the 52nd Session of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in the Iraqi capital Baghdad, according to a statement by the Iranian Foreign Ministry.
"Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation," he said.
Araghchi reaffirmed Iran's commitment to safe and secure navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, noting the waterway was open before the United States and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.
He said Iran has conveyed a "concrete" seven-day plan to the United States through Qatar, under which, if the necessary conditions are met, the strait could be reopened within seven days.
"The choice now rests with the United States," the minister added.
Araghchi stressed that Iran will continue to defend its people, sovereignty and legitimate interests by any means, and that it has never attacked its neighbors, only the U.S. military bases and installations in those states. He stressed that each regional state's territory, airspace and infrastructure should be used only to serve regional security and never as a platform for attacks on a neighbor.
"No state can build lasting security at the expense of the security of others," Araghchi said. "We believe the problems of our region are best resolved within the region, by its own states, before they become a pretext for the wars of distant powers."
On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.
A ceasefire was achieved between the warring parties on April 8. On June 18, Iran and the United States signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on ending the war in the region on all fronts.
Under the MoU, the two countries were scheduled to hold negotiations within 60 days, ending on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement on Iran's nuclear program and the removal of sanctions. However, they failed to make sufficient progress toward a deal as tensions continued to escalate. ■

articles.title: The language of extermination: NAZA, Artificial Intelligence and Gaza
articles.body:
The 80-minute documentary NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, is chastening. It examines the conduct of the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) during its ferocious, unremitting war in Gaza, drawing upon the interviews of 24 anonymised military and intelligence personnel. The interviews were filmed on Tel Aviv rooftops at night, with profiles and voices appropriately altered. The name of the documentary draws on a Hebrew acronym for nezek agavi or collateral damage, an obscene term used when counting the estimated number of civilians who will perish in a military strike. Last month, the film won the Special Jury Prize at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, receiving a standing ovation lasting 25 minutes.
The interviewees focus on the terrifyingly relevant role played by Artificial Intelligence (AI) targeting systems used in guiding the bombing campaign launched in response to the Hamas-led attacks of 7th October 2023. In Abraham’s words, “the Israeli intelligence officers we spoke with talked to us about how this mass killing is systemic: not by accident, but by design, actions of murder and policies that are based on the total dehumanisation of Palestinians.”
One of the interviewed subjects speaks of the goal being “quantity, not quality.” Another notes the conscious decision to target Hamas members, some even in the lower echelons, when they would be at home even if it meant killing family members and neighbours.
In one recalled instance, the phone of a 12-year-old girl was hacked to learn when her father would arrive home. The subsequent strike killed her. The cold logic is revealed in the rhetorical question posed by one of the interviewees: “When people talk about ‘flattening Gaza,’ what do you mean if not executing people?’
Despite being placed in a “too hot to handle” category by prominent indie studios, the self-distributed documentary managed to pass the US$500,000 mark in the United States after two weeks of release. Eight days after premiering at New York’s IFC Center, it went on to earn US$125,000. A further 85 theatres across 30 cities across North America then showed the film. Michelle Goldberg, writing in The New York Times, was impressed by the drawing power of the production when attending Walter Reade Theater for a screening. The venue, seating 268, was at capacity. “This is, in my experience, very unusual for documentaries of any sort, even those that, like ‘NAZA,’ win the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival.”
Militaries specialise in euphemised killing. A dedicated process of terminology and assessment sanitises and exsanguinates: death and murder become justifiable, necessary measures against an enemy bloated with wickedness and venality. In that process, mock tributes are paid to the canon of international law, notably international humanitarian law and doctrines of targeting. The more honest generals do us a favour by boasting about high casualty figures and mass mortality: they are not hiding matters and lurking behind worn ceremonies and the emperor’s non-existent clothes. Take the remarks of a former head of Israeli military intelligence made in a leaked audio: “For every one person [killed] on Oct. 7, 50 Palestinians must die.” Those militaries with a heavily staffed legal department supposedly providing guidance in striking a target, largely to reassure the squeamish that they are not implicated in acts of murder, are always suspect. In that regard, the IDF provides a model example, always claiming to do things differently from other powers in the region, yet resorting to the selective language of exculpation.
The reception of the film in Israel has been markedly hysterical. This was to be expected: the film unmasks and discomfits. It demolishes shibboleths. The IDF chief of staff Eyal Zamir vowed to use “every tool at our disposal” against the production. The Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar thought the film treasonous.
Abraham and Szor were “willing to harm their homeland in order just to get applause from antisemites around the world”. The irate minister was keen to “act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” he thundered in a social media post. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also called upon the passing of legislation stripping the duo of their citizenship, a curious point given the existing provisions of Israel’s Citizenship Law. (Making German Jews stateless was a specialty of the Third Reich: that the Jewish state would consider this to its citizens is a distinct, bitter irony, yet sadly permissible in light of the Israeli Supreme Court ruling in 2022 validating revocation for acts done in “breach of loyalty to the State of Israel”.)
Activists and members of the far-right party Jewish Power (Otzma Yehudit) led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir protested outside the parents of Szor’s house, with a speaker calling for both directors to be executed and the homes of their families to be demolished (collective punishment remains a great inspiration for tribal sentiment).
The IDF has marshalled its own response in a document accusing the filmmakers of presenting “a distorted, misleading and disingenuous picture of the IDF’s target planning and striking process.” The narrative of the documentary drew upon “substantial factual errors stemming from manipulative misrepresentations of reality.” Worth noting here is the lower register of critique that does not entirely repudiate the targeting practices of the IDF, dressed up in the apologetics of collateral damage. Concessions and confessions are always evident from those in and of power who resort to such dismissive language as “misrepresentative” and “disingenuous”.
Be that as it may, the agitated response is illuminating. The Lavender database, to take one objection, was apparently not one of targets, merely “a database that assists intelligence analysts.” This represents a distinction without a difference. The faith placed by militaries in the divinities of technology are hard to shake; there is nothing here to say that such analysts do not treat these data sets as unimpeachable. AI and religious deities serve to do the imagination for others; they discourage independent thinking and verification. Why bother when you have someone, or something else, doing it for you?
The response remains weak in claiming that the IDF believes itself “bound by and committed to international humanitarian law, its operational procedures are designed to implement those legal obligations, and it operates dedicated units and mechanisms to mitigate civilian harm.” The staggering death toll in Gaza, always sneered and jeered at by the Israeli authorities and their defenders, would suggest otherwise.
NAZA serves to, as the Israeli American historian Omer Bartov points out, address a “state of denial” by “actually speaking about the issue of what happened in Gaza rather than refusing to speak about it.”

articles.title: Taiwan tracks 14 Chinese ships, 2 military aircraft
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked two Chinese military aircraft, five naval vessels, and nine official ships between 6 a.m. on Saturday and the same time Sunday.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems. Two People’s Liberation Army aircraft sorties crossed the Taiwan Strait median line in the country’s northern and central air defense identification zones, according to the ministry.
So far this month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese aircraft 115 times and ships 208 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

articles.title: US Goes on the Offensive in Central Asia
articles.body:
It’s dealmaking time: despite the roiling geopolitical tensions embroiling Washington on several fronts, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio headed to Central and South Asia late Saturday to boost commercial ties – and gain an edge over Russia and China.
With the US mired in its war with Iran, and the conflict in Ukraine showing no signs of abating, Rubio has stepped up his foreign travel with recent trips to Europe and Latin America, smack in the middle of the US midterm election campaign.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He has largely ceded control of the contentious Iran, Ukraine and Gaza situations to US President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Rubio was instead leading a massive delegation of 200 business leaders to Uzbekistan, where he will take part on Monday in a ministerial meeting of five Central Asian countries.
“This is an important relationship,” Rubio said shortly before his departure, calling the trip a strategic visit. “There’s countries you’d like to get to because we want to build our relationships with them.”
A senior State Department official told reporters on Friday that Rubio was demonstrating Washington’s goodwill toward the “deepening partnership across Central Asia,” especially in the energy sector.
Central Asia is a resource-rich region as vast as the European Union but only boasts a population of about 80 million people.
White House Defends Russia Sanctions Waiver to Aid Peace Talks
“We’ve been planning this for several months, and it’s an incredible opportunity to bring the United States into a region of the world that is vitally important,” said a second senior US official, on condition of anonymity.
During his visit to the Uzbek city of Samarkand, an emblematic stop on the historic Silk Road, Rubio will participate in a C5+1 meeting with ministers from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
In November 2025, Trump welcomed the leaders of those countries to the White House.
The former Soviet republics remain linked to Moscow by energy pipelines, as well as security and migratory networks, but Russian influence has eroded since the start of the war in Ukraine -- with China reaping the benefits.
Beijing is the main trade partner of all five Central Asian nations.
Chinese companies have signed a number of energy-related deals, seeking to buy natural gas in Turkmenistan, uranium in Kazakhstan and rare earths in Tajikistan.
The US also has made sourcing rare earths and improving its energy mix key parts of its foreign policy.
The US ambassador to India, Sergio Gor – who also serves as the special envoy for Central and South Asia -- has repeatedly emphasized the need for Washington to have better ties across the region.
Trade deal
After his visit to Uzbekistan, Rubio will head to India, with stops in Mumbai and Jamnagar in Gujarat state. Both are industrial hubs and major international port cities.
It will be the secretary of state’s second official visit to India this year, after a May trip to New Delhi and Kolkata, signifying Washington’s push in the region.
“We’re very close” to a trade deal with India, the second senior US official said of negotiations that have dragged on for months.
Last February, the two sides reached a provisional agreement aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian products.
But just a few days later, the US Supreme Court struck down many of Trump’s tariffs, which fueled uncertainty about when a bilateral trade deal could take effect.
Ever since, Washington and Delhi have been locked in negotiations.
Relations were rattled when Trump imposed 25 percent tariffs on Indian goods in retaliation for Delhi’s purchases of Russian oil, but those duties have since been lifted.
In Mumbai and Jamnagar, Rubio will offer the new US brand of so-called “commercial diplomacy” in his meetings with Indian business leaders.
He will notably raise plans by the Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries to finance a refinery in Texas. Reliance is led by billionaire Indian tycoon Anant Ambani.

articles.title: Iran's parliament approves Mehrdad Akhlachi as defense minister after predecessor killed by Israel
articles.body:
Iran's parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlachi Ketabchi as defense minister on Sunday, ending months of interim leadership at the ministry and placing a former defense sector veteran in charge of the country's defense production and procurement apparatus.
Akhlachi replaces Majid Ebn al-Reza, who took over in an interim capacity after then Defense Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed by US-Israeli strikes in February.
Akhlachi has spent decades in Iran's defense industry and has held senior roles in its aerospace and missile sectors. He is subject to US and EU sanctions over his work in Iran's defense sector.
In a program presented to lawmakers, Akhlachi pledged to rebuild the country's military-industrial infrastructure, accelerate the development of defense technologies and expand cooperation with private-sector companies.
"If the American enemy makes another miscalculation, the response of the valiant Iranian people and the fighters of Islam will be surprising and extensive," he said, adding that Tehran had taken necessary measures to counter the potential use by the US of its "mother of all bombs" against Iran.
US planning to use MOAB against Iran
CNN reported this week that the US has developed strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known as the "mother of all bombs," against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders renewed combat operations.
The weapon is one of the largest non-nuclear bombs in the US arsenal.
"The US President should focus on ensuring his forces are withdrawn safely from our region. If he drops a single bomb, he will have to see how many of his troops end up being carried out of the region in a horizontal position," Akhlachi said.

articles.title: Rubio heads to Central Asia while other US officials hit foreign policy hot spots
articles.body:
Rubio heads to Central Asia while other US officials hit foreign policy hot spots
WASHINGTON, Oct 18 - While the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights the Houthis and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio travels on Sunday to Uzbekistan, a nation far removed from the biggest US foreign policy challenges.
The top US diplomat is scheduled to land in Samarkand on Sunday to meet with leaders from the C5+1, a grouping that brings together the United States and the Muslim-majority post-Soviet states of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
US officials have portrayed resource-rich Central Asia — the region between China, Russia and Iran — as worthy of more attention than it received from US President Donald Trump's predecessors.
Trump hosted C5 leaders at the White House last November, when Kazakhstan agreed to join the Abraham Accords, a series of agreements under which Muslim-majority countries have normalized or deepened relations with Israel. Separately, Trump met with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev at the United Nations General Assembly last September.
Regional politics aside, the trip fits an emerging pattern in which Rubio often visits regions not at the center of the news cycle, while leaving some more fraught foreign-policy portfolios to other Trump aides, including special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President JD Vance.
For instance, Rubio has not visited Kyiv or Moscow since becoming secretary of state. He was not present for talks between US and Ukrainian officials in Florida earlier this month, when US officials pressed Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries. Vance, not Rubio, represented the US in Pakistan during peace talks with Iran in April.
Rubio's previous foreign trip, in early October, took him to Greece, Portugal and Iceland.
Trump administration officials have typically rejected any suggestion that cabinet-level officials should focus their travels on geopolitical capitals and hot spots.
Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, for instance, said on X last week that the idea only certain destinations were worthy of visits from secretaries of state "perfectly encapsulates the decadence and degeneracy of the contemporary US foreign policy establishment."
US-RUSSIA RELATIONS LOOM
One Central Asian diplomat, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said officials in the region are wondering to what extent the US will continue targeting Russian sanctions evasion. All C5 states, while drawing closer to the US, have deep historical ties with Moscow, and the region has facilitated Russian imports and exports that violate US and European Union sanctions, Western officials say.
In the past, the US has pushed regional states to clamp down on those illicit flows.
But Trump struck a deal with Moscow this month to import Russian diesel, a move to lower domestic fuel prices before the congressional midterm elections. On Friday, Trump waived all provisions of legislation that would have allowed him to slap massive tariffs on some nations that buy significant amounts of Russian crude or otherwise help Moscow evade sanctions. Among the nations that could have been affected, experts have said, are India and Kazakhstan.
India, which Rubio will visit after Uzbekistan, remains the world's No. 2 Russian crude importer after China, despite Trump saying in February that India had agreed to stop buying oil from Russia.
Additional questions hang over a potential trade deal with India and an expansion of the Abraham Accords in Central Asia.
A US official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, described the trade deal on Friday as "pretty much done," raising the possibility that an agreement could be announced during the Rubio trip.
Separately, the US has talked to additional Central Asian nations about joining the Abraham Accords, Reuters reported last year, conversations that could in theory continue in Samarkand.
More than 200 business executives will accompany Rubio to Uzbekistan, the State Department said. The Central Asian diplomat said the Trump administration has focused its commercial efforts on expanding access to the area's rare earth mineral resources.
The trip to Uzbekistan was largely organized by Sergio Gor, the US ambassador to India, the Central Asian diplomat said. Gor, who was born in Uzbekistan and is a friend of Rubio, also serves as the US special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs.
After Uzbekistan, Rubio will visit the Indian cities of Mumbai and Jamnagar to meet with business leaders, including Reliance Industries Chairman Mukesh Ambani, who earned the Trump administration's favor earlier in the year by backing a new refinery in Texas. Rubio most recently visited India five months ago.
The trip is due to wrap up on Thursday. REUTERS

articles.title: All-front ceasefire essential to ending regional war
articles.body:
In an interview with Lebanon’s Al Mayadeen television network on Friday, Khatibzadeh – who arrived in Beirut on Wednesday for talks with Lebanese officials – said Iran remained committed to ending the Israeli war on Lebanon and had secured this objective in the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, which Iran and the United States signed in mid-June this year.
He said Lebanon was among the key issues discussed between Iran and the US, adding that he sought to bring the two sides closer during his visit to Beirut. Khatibzadeh said that he held “good” talks with Lebanese officials, including Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, and officials at the Foreign Ministry.

The Iranian diplomat also said that Washington and Tel Aviv violated the Islamabad understanding through their attacks on Iran and Lebanon, adding that US efforts to secure a ceasefire and end Israel’s war on Lebanon had reached a deadlock. Khatibzadeh described the US war against Iran as illegal under international law, saying Washington had failed to destroy Iran’s air defenses and deterrence capabilities. He said Iran had resisted an existential war and would continue defending its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
He added that Tehran was ready to address concerns raised by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the United States over Iran’s peaceful nuclear activities, citing more than 15 IAEA reports that he said confirmed Iran’s compliance with its commitments.

articles.title: Taiwan top security official speaks at Berlin forum
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) told a forum in Berlin that peace in the Taiwan Strait also affects Europe’s security and economy, reports said Saturday.
Wu was speaking at the Taiwan Forum Thursday organized by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, a thinktank allied with Germany’s Free Democratic Party. He compared Taiwan’s situation with Ukraine facing the Russian invasion, per CNA.
Conflict in the Taiwan Strait will impact European industry and disrupt global supply chains, the former foreign minister said. He also called for closer Taiwan-EU cooperation in the fields of cyber security, AI, and semiconductors.
European Parliament Committee on Security and Defense Chair Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann said most European countries supported Taiwan, but in different ways. Germany’s problem was that its economy was too reliant on China, she said, adding that Beijing was watching how the EU responded to the war in Ukraine.
Wu said that Taiwan was facing a difficult choice in how to react to China’s actions in the region, including its repeated military drills and incursions into Taiwanese restricted waters and Air Defense Identification Zone, CNA reported. A response might raise regional tension, but not responding would lead China to increase the pressure, he said.
Wu said Taiwan will not rely on other countries, but shoulder its responsibility to defend its freedom, sovereignty, and democratic system. The country will continue to improve its defense capabilities and deter regional conflict with its democratic partners, the top national security official said.

articles.title: Singularities: von Neumann, Good, Vinge, …
articles.body:
Singularities: von Neumann, Good, Vinge, …
« previous post |
The OED gives citations for singularity going back to the 14th century, e.g. this example from 1398 in the sense "The fact or condition of being alone or apart from others; solitariness":
Men vsyd to ete togyders in open place, leest syngularite schuld brede lechery.
A mathematical singularity, as Wikipedia tells us,"is a point at which a given mathematical object is not defined, or a point where the mathematical object ceases to be well-behaved in some particular way, such as by lacking differentiability or analyticity", with an obvious example being what happens to the reciprocal function 1/x at the point x=0. I'm not sure when that usage began, but it's easy to find references back to the 19th century, e.g. Charlotte Angas Scott, "On the higher singularities of plane curves", American Journal of Mathematics 1892.
Most uses of the term these days involve a metaphorical extension of the mathematical concept to the idea of a technological singularity, which Wikipedia describes as "a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization."
The first documented use of this metaphor is attributed to John von Neumann in a 1958 posthumous tribute by Stanislaw Ulam:
Quite aware that the criteria of value in mathematical work are, to some extent, purely aesthetic, he once expressed an apprehension that the values put on abstract scientific achievement in our present civilization might diminish: "The interests of humanity may change, the present curiosities in science may cease, and entirely different things may occupy the human mind in the future." One conversation centered on the ever accelerating progress of technology and changes in the mode of human life, which gives the appearance of approaching some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue.
Then in the early 1960s, I.J. Good presented "Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine". Good doesn't use the term singularity, but he clearly expresses (a version of) the idea. From his Introduction:
Let an ultraintelligent machine be defined as a machine that can far surpass all the intellectual activities of any man however clever. Since the design of machines is one of these intellectual activities, an ultraintelligent machine could design even better machines; there would then unquestionably be an 'intelligence explosion', and the intelligence of man would be left far behind. Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.
And from his Conclusion:
It is more probable than not that, within the twentieth century, an ultraintelligent machine will be built and that it will be the last invention that man need make, since it will lead to an "intelligence explosion." This will transform society in an unimaginable way. The first ultraintelligent machine will need to be ultraparallel, and is likely to be achieved with the help of a very large artificial neural net. […] The machine will have a multimillion dollar computer and information-retrieval system under its direct control. The design of the machine will be partly suggested by analogy with several aspects of the human brain and intellect. In particular, the machine will have high linguistic ability and will be able to operate with the meanings of propositions, because to do so will lead to a necessary economy, just as it does in man.
The whole article is well worth reading carefully, and it's a scandal that the only available (and somewhat corrupted) version is on the Wayback Machine. For more on I.J. Good, see my 2009 post "Good is dead", which sketches his contributions (with Alan Turing) to the world's first Language Model, as part of the Enigma decryption effort more than 80 years ago.
The next step (that I know of) was taken by Vernor Vinge, in a 1983 op-ed in Omni Magazine (I've typed out the contents because the original, black type on a dark grey background, is hard to read):
A favorite game of futurists is to plot technological performance – computer speed, say – against time. Such trend curves climb ever more steeply. Extrapolated 30 or 40 years, they are so high and steep that even the most naive futurist discounts their accuracy. Some who talk about that era predict a leveling off of progress. After all, saturation effects are observed in other growth processes.
There is an important reason why this process won’t level off. We are at the point of accelerating the evolution of intelligence itself. The exact means of accomplishing this phenomenon cannot yet be predicted – and is not important. Whether our work is case in silicon or DNA will have little effect on the ultimate results. The evolution of human intelligence took millions of years. We will devise an equivalent advance in a fraction of that time. We will soon create intelligences greater than our own.
When this happens, human history will have reached a kind of singularity, an intellectual transition as impenetrable as the knotted space-time at the center of a black hole, and the world will pass far beyond our understanding. This singularity, I believe, already haunts a number of science-fiction writers. It makes realistic extrapolations to an interstellar future impossible. To write a story set more than a century hence, one needs a nuclear war in between – to retard progress enough so that the world remains intelligible.
In a 1993 article "Technological Singularity", still (for now) available on the web, Vinge elevates singularity into the title. He quotes Ulam/von Neumann and Good, and concludes by speculating about "the Best We Can Ask For". The whole thing is worth reading.
It's striking how accurately some recent developments were foreseen by von Neumann and Good and Vinge 30-70 years ago — but what strikes me most about the current situation is how much of it was not predicted. None of those seers told us about Data Center politics; AI hallucinations; the socio-political and cybersecurity effects of AI bots and agentic AI; the economics of a possible AI bubble; and so on.
Maybe this is just temporary turbulence as a smoothly-flowing post-singularity future is forming, whether utopian or dystopian or both. But from where I sit, the foreseeable future of (things called) "AI" looks even more chaotic, which is one more reason to doubt that the concept of a singularity is really helpful.
A different metaphor is implied by Richard Dooling's 2009 book Rapture for the Geeks , as well as a 2012 work the rapture of the nerds by Cory Doctorow and Charles Stross. Both allude to the (religious) Rapture, which is conceived in many different ways by different individuals and groups, but is generally seen as an abrupt event that's positioned in the middle of other variously defined and described times, and affects different groups of people in very different ways.

articles.title: Ukraine prepares two low-cost domestic missiles for combat use against jet-powered Geran drones
articles.body:
Ukraine prepares two low-cost domestic missiles for combat use against jet-powered Geran drones
Two Ukrainian teams are preparing domestically developed surface-to-air missiles for combat use against Russian jet-powered drones.
Source: Andrii Hrytseniuk, head of the Ukrainian defence-tech cluster Brave1, in an interview with Ukrainska Pravda
Details: "They are cheap and easy to manufacture. One of the requirements was to keep the cost of a missile below US$20,000," Hrytseniuk said.
The ambition of these projects is underscored by the average market cost of missiles, ranging from hundreds of thousands of dollars per shot for a Stinger to half a million dollars for an AIM-9X missile used by F-16 fighter jets.
Even using two or three such missiles against a Russian long-range drone is expected to be cost-effective relative to the value of the target. Various estimates put the cost of a standard Geran at around US$70,000, while its jet-powered version may cost tens of thousands of dollars more.
Hrytseniuk said Brave1 began funding the development of surface-to-air missiles in 2024. It took two years to produce the first prototypes. A total of 10 Ukrainian teams are working on such missiles.
Background: In May, it was reported that Ukraine is developing low-cost interceptor missiles and had already tested some solutions. Then-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said there were plans to scale up their production dozens of times.

Russia has attacked Ukraine's energy sector 76 times since Trump announced truce, Zelenskyy says

My condolences to their families and loved ones. This morning, there was a strike on an agricultural enterprise in Volyn."

The president said Russia is trying to plunge Ukraine into a blackout.
"And America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," Zelenskyy wrote.

articles.title: Ukraine FM says Russian-held town is a 'death trap' with starving residents, Zelensky says genocide
articles.body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Saturday that Russian occupying forces were turning the Ukrainian town of Oleshky into a "death trap" gripped by starvation, and urged international organizations to help evacuate its residents.
Sybiha made his comments on X/Twitter a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin pledged, in a conversation with Pope Leo, to cooperate in delivering vital supplies into the town in southern Ukraine's Kherson region.
"Russians are trying to turn the Ukrainian town of Oleshky into a death trap. The hospital has run out of medicine. Dozens of bodies lie in the streets or in homes, as Russians forbid residents from burying them," Sybiha wrote.
"Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, preserves and even snails... Ukraine has repeatedly called for safe evacuation and international humanitarian access. These appeals cannot remain unanswered."
The Kremlin acknowledged in September that Oleshky had critical problems with food and medical supplies but said Russia's military was working to resolve them. Ukraine's military has twice used drones to deliver food and medicine to the town.
UN, Red Cross urged to secure evacuations, humanitarian access
Sybiha urged the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and other organizations to "secure safe evacuation corridors and immediate humanitarian access."
Oleshky lies on the east side of the Dnipro River in the Kherson region, which Russian forces mostly occupied soon after the 2022 invasion. A Ukrainian counteroffensive later recaptured large chunks of territory, including the city of Kherson.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy described the situation in Oleshky this week as "genocide."
Oleshky had a pre-war population of 24,000 people and is now home to around 1,700 residents, including 47 children, according to Danielle Bell, head of the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.
Local prosecutors said on Saturday Russian forces dropped aerial bombs on the city of Kherson, on the opposite bank of the Dnipro from Oleshky, killing an ambulance driver and wounding 40 people.

articles.title: Drones Hit St. Petersburg Oil Terminals, VK Data Center, and Bridge
articles.body:
A Ukrainian drone attack early Sunday morning, Oct. 18, struck fuel transshipment infrastructure, a major enterprise data center, a logistics warehouse, and a highway bridge across St. Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad region, sparking multiple fires and knocking out power to 20,000 residents.
St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed that the municipality came under attack by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) overnight, resulting in blazes across four city districts.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Beglov acknowledged impacts at the Petersburg Oil Terminal (PNT) alongside damage to additional infrastructure sites, while claiming that emergency responders had been dispatched to contain localized fires.
According to independent Russian outlet Astra, municipal emergency warning systems failed to notify residents ahead of the strikes, with alerts transmitted either after impacts had occurred or with substantial operational delays.
Open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis conducted by Astra verified that fires erupted at the Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Baltic region’s primary petroleum transshipment hub.
Concurrently in the city’s Krasnogvardeisky district, drone debris ignited a blaze at the “Ruchyi” oil depot. The Ruchyi fuel depot maintains an operational capacity of 3,900 cubic meters, functioning as a bulk storage and loading facility for AI-92 and AI-95 gasoline alongside commercial diesel.
Mushrooms and the Autumn Moon
Hits on VK data center, substation, and Ozon logistics depot
The overnight assault extended across the administrative boundary into the Leningrad region, targeting corporate digital backbones and electrical distribution facilities.
In the village of Novosergievka in the Vsevolozhsk district, strike drones hit a large server data center owned by Russian technology giant VK (VKontakte).
Although VK company representatives claimed corporate services continued operating normally, users across Russia reported widespread connection dropouts and outages affecting the VKontakte social media platform and its integrated ecosystem.
Astra’s OSINT analysts established that an electrical substation located adjacent to the VK data center was also damaged during the strike.
Leningrad Region Governor Alexander Drozdenko confirmed that damage to electrical distribution installations triggered emergency power cuts, leaving approximately 20,000 residents in the area without electricity.
Separately, Russian e-commerce company Ozon confirmed that an aerial impact sparked a fire at its fulfillment center in St. Petersburg’s Kolpino district on Sofiyskaya Street.
Operating as one of Ozon’s busiest logistics facilities in northwestern Russia, the hub spans up to 79,000 square meters.
The company reported that emergency brigades contained the blaze and confirmed no personnel were injured.
Strike on Western High-Speed Diameter bridge
Drone impacts were also recorded on municipal transport arteries. According to Astra, a drone struck the cable-stayed bridge spanning the Korabelny fairway in St. Petersburg, located roughly 4.5 kilometers from the Petersburg Oil Terminal.
The bridge forms a critical section of the southern viaduct of the Western High-Speed Diameter (WHSD), a multi-lane toll expressway connecting northern and southern sectors of the metropolis.
Municipal engineering teams were deployed to evaluate structural damage to the suspension cables and road deck.
The multi-site strikes in St. Petersburg and Leningrad region reflect an expanding Ukrainian asymmetric campaign to degrade Russian rear logistics, petroleum transshipment, and corporate digital logistics.
The incident follows consecutive strikes on Russian technology hubs earlier in the month, including attacks that disabled Yandex data centers in Vladimir, Ryazan, and Kaluga regions, alongside reported strikes on a Sberbank data center facility in Saratov region.
