articles.title: For Israel, Greece is more than a friend - it is a strategic partner - opinion
articles.body:
In the Middle East, where alliances are repeatedly tested by crises, Greece is a partner Israel should value.
Beyond the blue sea, the islands, and the beloved music stands a country that understands the importance of its relationship with Israel and gives it diplomatic, security, and economic depth.
Relations between Jerusalem and Athens show how geographic proximity can become a strategic partnership when political leaders invest in it over time.
Relations between countries also have a personal dimension, expressed through diplomatic encounters.
One such occasion was a dinner hosted by Ami H Orkaby, dean of the Israeli Consular Corps and honorary consul general of South Korea, and his wife, Shirley.
Gil Haskel, Israel’s chief of protocol, attended the dinner, which was held in honor of Nikolaos Margaropoulos of Greece, president of the World Federation of Consuls (FICAC).
Such gatherings illustrate the importance of diplomacy in connecting people and countries, building relationships, and cultivating trust.
The organization president’s Greek background also gives the occasion a personal connection to relations with Greece. Honorary consuls, who operate at the intersection of diplomacy and business, can help expand relationships and advance new initiatives.
Alongside formal agreements, hospitality, conversation, and a willingness to listen and help create the foundation for future partnerships, Orkaby’s contribution to cultivating these encounters and strengthening Israel’s international relationships deserves recognition.
What makes Greek-Israeli ties so significant
Greece’s approach toward Israel is especially worthy of appreciation because it exists within a complex political reality. Friendship does not require agreement on every issue.
Athens maintains independent positions and has criticized Israel on diplomatic matters, but disagreements do not erase the relationship’s importance.
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis’s visit to Israel in October 2023, following the Hamas attack, expressed solidarity during an exceptionally difficult period and demonstrated the human significance of the partnership.
Greece’s ambassador to Israel, Maya Solomou, also deserves recognition for her contribution to this continuing effort. She presented her credentials to President Isaac Herzog in February 2025.
Her work demonstrates the value of diplomacy that connects governments, business communities, and professionals.
Her presence in economic and security forums provides an active point of contact and helps turn goodwill into meetings, new relationships, and the exploration of practical opportunities for cooperation.
In January 2026, Solomou was the guest of honor at a meeting of the Israel Greece Chamber of Commerce’s security, policing and cybersecurity forum. She emphasized the trust between the countries and the importance of expanding their economic and technological ties.
The chamber also published an invitation to a business meeting at her residence in June.
These are examples of diplomacy’s practical contribution: opening doors, bringing entrepreneurs together, and strengthening mutual familiarity. Her investment in making this friendship part of everyday life deserves appreciation.
The security partnership offers particularly impressive examples.
The international flight training center in Kalamata, established and operated by Elbit Systems under an agreement between the two countries’ defense ministries, combines Israeli experience with the needs of the Hellenic Air Force.
Training aircraft, instructional systems, and simulators create professional infrastructure for the long term.
The project’s significance extends beyond a commercial transaction: it reflects Greece’s willingness to entrust a central component of its pilot training program to a reliable partner.
JOINT MILITARY exercises provide another important dimension.
In September 2023, the IDF described an aerial exercise with Greece that included long-range flights, aerial refueling, low-altitude flying, and deploying munitions at Greek training ranges.
Exercises of this kind allow both sides to learn from each other and become familiar with diverse operational conditions.
The 2026 military cooperation program among Israel, Greece, and Cyprus demonstrates that the relationship is also expanding into an organized regional framework based on planning and coordination.
Alongside aircraft and military exercises, the friendship also has a distinctly civilian dimension. In the summer of 2023, Israel sent firefighting aircraft and crews to help Greece confront severe wildfires.
When communities, forests, and human lives are in danger, cooperation gains tangible meaning. Operational expertise and the ability to mobilize quickly demonstrate how a relationship between countries can provide direct assistance to people in need.
Tourism is another central pillar of the relationship. Proximity, culture, and Greek hospitality create a natural foundation for encounters between the two peoples, along with economic opportunities in hospitality, aviation, and related services.
In September 2026, the Greek tourism minister and Israel’s ambassador in Athens discussed expanding tourism cooperation. This continued engagement has considerable value. Every successful personal encounter can strengthen familiarity, reduce suspicion, and generate mutual interest.
Energy, water, and innovation offer more opportunities for progress. Joint business forums are exploring ways to connect Israeli technological capabilities with opportunities in Greece and Cyprus.
Energy connectivity projects still require economic evaluation, financing, and solutions to diplomatic challenges, but the coordination itself is important.
It allows the countries to think regionally about energy security, supply diversification, and stronger links between the Eastern Mediterranean and Europe.
This is also where the significance of the trilateral partnership with Cyprus and the cooperative framework with the United States becomes clear. These relationships can serve as a counterweight to exert pressure in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Amid disputes with Turkey over maritime boundaries and energy resources, coordination strengthens the negotiating position of the participating countries.
In the face of the Iranian threat and regional attacks on trade routes, stable security relationships become even more important.
Greece pursues an independent foreign policy, and the trilateral relationship should not be interpreted as a threat to other countries.
Its strength lies in responsible deterrence: protecting sovereignty, infrastructure, and freedom of navigation while leaving the door open to dialogue.
Successful cooperation increases the prospects for regional stability.
Greece deserves a central place in Israel’s foreign policy and treatment that recognizes both its contribution and its needs.
The work of Solomou, the efforts of professional officials, and the political commitment in both capitals give the partnership an opportunity to continue deepening.
In an era of uncertainty, knowing that a country across the sea stands ready to train, trade, innovate, and exchange assistance is a genuine strategic asset.
That asset should be cultivated wisely, with mutual respect and gratitude. It is an investment in our security, our economy, and the ability of future generations to live in a stable and prosperous region.
The writer is the CEO of Radios 100FM, an Honorary Consul and vice dean of the Consular Diplomatic Corps, president of the Israel Amateur Radio Club, and previously served as a monitor for Israel Army Radio and as a television correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title: US goes on the offensive in Central Asia
articles.body:
US goes on the offensive in Central Asia
- Marco Rubio is visiting Central and South Asia to strengthen US trade ties and counter Russia and China, with a 200-strong business delegation and a C5+1 meeting in Uzbekistan.
- Central Asia is rich in energy and minerals, but China is now its main trade partner. The US wants better access to rare earths and stronger energy links.
- Rubio will then visit India, where Washington says it is “very close” to a trade deal. Talks continue after tariff disputes and tensions over India’s Russian oil purchases.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – It is deal-making time: Despite the roiling geopolitical tensions embroiling Washington on several fronts, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio headed to Central and South Asia late on Oct 17 to boost commercial ties – and gain an edge over Russia and China.
With the US mired in its war with Iran, and the conflict in Ukraine showing no signs of abating, Rubio has stepped up his foreign travel with recent trips to Europe and Latin America, smack in the middle of the US midterm polls campaign.
He has largely ceded control of the contentious Iran, Ukraine and Gaza situations to US President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Rubio was instead leading a massive delegation of 200 business leaders to Uzbekistan, where he will take part in a ministerial meeting of five Central Asian countries on Oct 19.
“This is an important relationship,” he said shortly before his departure, calling the trip a strategic visit. “There’s countries you’d like to get to because we want to build our relationships with them.”
A senior State Department official told reporters on Oct 16 that Rubio was demonstrating Washington’s goodwill towards the “deepening partnership across Central Asia”, especially in the energy sector.
Central Asia is a resource-rich region as vast as the European Union but has a population of only about 80 million people.
“We’ve been planning this for several months, and it’s an incredible opportunity to bring the United States into a region of the world that is vitally important,” said a second senior US official, on condition of anonymity.
During his visit to the Uzbek city of Samarkand, an emblematic stop on the historic Silk Road, Rubio will participate in a C5+1 meeting with ministers from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
In November 2025, Trump welcomed the leaders of those countries to the White House.
The former Soviet republics remain linked to Moscow by energy pipelines, as well as security and migratory networks, but Russian influence has eroded since the start of the war in Ukraine – with China reaping the benefits.
Beijing is the main trade partner of all five Central Asian nations.
Chinese companies have signed a number of energy-related deals, seeking to buy natural gas in Turkmenistan, uranium in Kazakhstan and rare earths in Tajikistan.
The US also has made sourcing rare earths and improving its energy mix key parts of its foreign policy.
The US Ambassador to India, Sergio Gor – who also serves as the special envoy for Central and South Asia – has repeatedly emphasised the need for Washington to have better ties across the region.
Trade deal
After his visit to Uzbekistan, Rubio will head to India, with stops in Mumbai and Jamnagar in Gujarat state. Both are industrial hubs and major international port cities.
It will be the Secretary of State’s second official visit to India in 2026, after a May trip to New Delhi and Kolkata, signifying Washington’s push in the region.
“We’re very close” to a trade deal with India, the second senior US official said of negotiations that have dragged on for months.
In February, the two sides reached a provisional agreement aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian products.
But just a few days later, the US Supreme Court struck down many of Trump’s tariffs, which fuelled uncertainty about when a bilateral trade deal could take effect.
Ever since, Washington and Delhi have been locked in negotiations.
Relations were rattled when Trump imposed 25% tariffs on Indian goods in retaliation for Delhi’s purchases of Russian oil, but those duties have since been lifted.
In Mumbai and Jamnagar, Rubio will offer the new US brand of so-called “commercial diplomacy” in his meetings with Indian business leaders.
He will notably raise plans by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries to finance a refinery in Texas. Reliance is led by billionaire Indian tycoon Anant Ambani. AFP

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts two Houthi ballistic missiles, four drones
articles.body:
The Saudi-led coalition said on Sunday it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by Houthi militias towards Khamis Mushait in southwestern Saudi Arabia.
Coalition spokesperson Turki al Maliki announced the interceptions in a statement on X.
Shortly before the announcement, Saudi Civil Defense issued “potential danger” alerts in Riyadh and the southwestern cities of Abha and Khamis Mushait through its national early warning system. The agency later said the danger had passed.
On Saturday, al Maliki said coalition forces had also intercepted and destroyed four drones over several hours in the Riyadh region, the Eastern Province and southern Saudi Arabia.
The coalition released footage it said showed strikes destroying two ballistic missile launchers in Saada, northern Yemen, after they had been used to fire missiles towards Saudi Arabia.
The developments come amid continued military escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia since July, including attacks targeting civilian aviation facilities and energy infrastructure in the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition since March 2015 in support of Yemen’s internationally recognised government against the Houthis, who have controlled the capital Sanaa and several other provinces since September 2014.

articles.title: Iran rejects pressure, remains open to dialogue: Araghchi
articles.body:
Addressing the 52nd Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in Baghdad, Araghchi said Iran did not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, stressing that any dialogue must be grounded in mutual respect and backed by credible guarantees.
The full text of his speech is as follows:
In the Name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful
Excellency, Mr. Fuad Mohammed Hussein, Deputy Prime Minister, and Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Iraq,
Mr. Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed, Secretary-General of the OIC,
Excellencies,
Ladies and Gentlemen,
I begin by thanking the Government and people of the Republic of Iraq, our neighbor and brother, for hosting this meeting of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation and for their warm hospitality. I congratulate Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed for his appointment as the new Secretary-General, and wish him full success. I also thank the Republic of Tyrkiya for all its efforts during its successful chairmanship of the OIC CFM. Moreover, I should thank the Secretary-General and the General Secretariat for their efforts in preparing this meeting.
It is fitting that we gather in a land that has long been a meeting place of civilizations, at a time when unity and dialogue within the Islamic world are needed more than ever.
The OIC was founded to give the Islamic Ummah a common voice and to promote solidarity, cooperation and the defense of our shared interests. Keeping the path of dialogue open among us is not weakness. It is a responsibility. The Charter of our Organization rests on principles that reflect those contained in the UN Charter: sovereign equality, territorial integrity, non-interference in internal affairs, peaceful settlement of disputes, and refraining from the threat or use of force. These principles belong to no single country or group of countries. They protect all of us, and when they are applied selectively, they lose their value.
Dear Brothers and Sisters,
Iran has been steadfast in its commitment to international law, the UN Charter and diplomacy. Over the past two years we continued to pursue diplomacy. The United States chose the opposite path: aggression, threats, assassination and economic warfare, with a blatant disregard for international law and the UN Charter. About five thousand people were killed as martyrs, including hundreds of women and children. The United States and the Israeli regime assassinated Iran's Supreme Leader and other senior political and military officials, a grave violation of international law. The killing of more than 160 students and teachers in Minab, the cluster-munition attack on the Lamerd stadium, the bombing of a desalination unit in Qeshm and the attack on a wedding ceremony in Kuhestak, Sirik, are only some of the documented examples. The United States and the Israeli regime cannot whitewash these crimes by reversing the roles of victim and aggressor. I thank those member states that have expressed solidarity with the Iranian people in these difficult times, and I call on the Organization as a whole to stand firmly against attacks on the sovereignty and territorial integrity of its founding member.
Iran defended its people, its sovereignty and its legitimate interests, and will continue to do so by any means. We never attacked our neighbors, but we did attack and destroyed the US military bases and military installations, which are unfortunately, located in our neighborhood. But there is no contradiction between defending our rights and pursuing peace. We know the cost of war, and that is precisely why we value peace.
Iran asks for no special treatment, only the equal application of rights and responsibilities to all. This issue will not be resolved on the battlefield. Peace cannot be built through threats of annihilation.
Iran also remains committed to safe and secure navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway vital to the energy and trade of many of our member states. Until 28 February 2026, the Strait was open. The insecurity and disruption of maritime navigation since then are the direct result of the aggressive actions of the United States and the Israeli regime, and of the blockade and coercive measures imposed by the United States. Security cannot be restored by more of the same. One cannot bomb a country, threaten its annihilation and impose a blockade, and then expect the security of navigation return to normal.
Diplomacy was in fact working. Through the good offices of Pakistan, with the support of Qatar, both members of this Organization, Iran and the United States signed the Islamabad MoU on 17 June. Under paragraph 5, Iran undertook to make the necessary arrangements to facilitate the safe movement of vessels, and we immediately began technical discussions with the Sultanate of Oman to implement that commitment. Within two weeks, maritime traffic had recovered to approximately 60 percent of its pre-war level. Subsequent unilateral US measures and military action then blocked implementation of the Memorandum, and the dispute-resolution mechanisms it envisaged were bypassed.
Over the past two years, Iran has negotiated in good faith, and repeatedly, it was met with military action rather than diplomacy. This has created deep distrust about renewed negotiations without credible assurances against a repetition. Even so, Iran has kept the door open. Through Qatar, we have conveyed a concrete seven-day plan: if the necessary conditions are met, the Strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days. The choice now rests with the United States.
Excellencies,
The Palestinian cause remains the central cause of the Islamic world, and we cannot speak of peace while ignoring it. Palestine remains a wound on the conscience of the international community, and Gaza, a victim of genocide, has become a symbol of the failure of international mechanisms to protect civilians. Dozens of resolutions have not ended occupation and violence. The continuing suffering of the Palestinian people, the killing of innocent civilians by the Israeli regime and the threats to Al-Quds Al-Sharif and its holy sites should concern everyone. Iran stands with the Palestinian people, and we call on the OIC and all its members to do whatever it takes to put an end to the killing and the blockade and to make the protection of civilians and the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people a shared priority, backed by practical and coordinated action. And finally, I would like to endorse the proposal made by my brother, Hakan Fidan, the distinguished Foreign Minister of the Republic of Turkiya, to assign a day as Gaza Genocide Memorial Day.
On Yemen, for almost a decade, the people of Yemen have endured a devastating conflict, a prolonged blockade, and severe restrictions on vital civilian infrastructure. The role of the US and Israeli regime in inflicting suffering on Yemenis is undeniable. The resulting humanitarian catastrophe remains one of the gravest in the world, with serious violations of international humanitarian law continuing with impunity.
Iran's position is clear and unchanged. We support the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of Yemen, and those of the Saudi Arabia. We support a peaceful, inclusive and comprehensive political process as the only viable and sustainable means of resolving the conflict. Sustainable peace cannot be achieved through military escalation or coercion. There is no military solution.
The region's crises have no military solutions, and insisting on a military approach while disregarding a political solution only further complicates the situation. Iran is deeply concerned by developments in the Arabian Peninsula and remains ready to provide every assistance to facilitate dialogue between the parties, on the basis of the peace roadmap they previously agreed. The people of Yemen have the right to live with dignity, free from pressure, sanctions and blockade.
Dear Colleagues,
No state can build lasting security at the expense of the security of others. We believe the problems of our region are best resolved within the region, by its own states, before they become a pretext for the wars of distant powers. In that spirit, we believe the territory, airspace and infrastructure of every regional state should be used only to serve regional security and never become a platform for staging attacks on a neighbor. We say this in a spirit of brotherhood and good-neighborliness. Our peoples share one region and one future, and the choice before us is a simple one: either we build security together, or we will endure insecurity together. Iran stands ready to work with all its brothers and neighbors toward the former.
Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure. But we remain ready for dialogue based on mutual respect and credible guarantees.
I renew my thanks to our Iraqi hosts, and I wish this meeting success in serving the unity, peace, security and prosperity of the Islamic Ummah.
I thank you.
MNA

articles.title: Hegseth warns Iran to reach deal or face military action
articles.body:
AA Photo
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Oct. 17 Iran must abandon its nuclear ambitions and negotiate an agreement or face military action, presenting military pressure as essential to bringing Tehran to the negotiating table.
Speaking at the University of Tennessee, Hegseth said Iran could face "the kind of devastation that America can bring and will bring swiftly if necessary." His audience included military recruits and Reserve Officers’ Training Corps cadets.
He accused Iran of expanding its conventional missile forces to discourage intervention while pursuing nuclear ambitions. He also accused Tehran of financing Hezbollah and Yemen’s Houthis, saying Washington sought to deter attacks against American forces and shipping.
Hegseth placed the Iran policy within President Donald Trump’s broader push to reassert U.S. power. That effort, he said, included confronting drug cartels and reducing Iranian, Chinese and Russian influence in Latin America.
Turning to Venezuela, he described the country as a strategic partner with significant oil resources and said the American operation there would have consequences lasting generations.
Washington intended to remove rival powers from the Western Hemisphere while expanding its military presence and partnerships throughout the Americas, he said.

articles.title: Ceasefire must cover all fronts to end regional war, says diplomat
articles.body:
Ceasefire must cover all fronts to end regional war, says diplomat
TEHRAN— Iran has stressed that ending hostilities on all fronts is essential to achieving lasting peace in West Asia, warning that continued fighting in any part of the region would mean the war remains unresolved.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh made the remarks in an interview with Lebanon’s Al Mayadeen television network on Friday, emphasizing that an end to Israel’s war on Lebanon was integral to broader efforts to bring the regional conflict to a close.
Khatibzadeh, who arrived in Beirut on Wednesday for talks with Lebanese officials, said Iran remained committed to ending Israeli military aggression against Lebanon and had pursued that objective within the framework of the memorandum of understanding reached between Iran and the United States in Islamabad in mid-June.
He described Lebanon as one of the key issues discussed in Iran’s engagements with Washington, adding that his visit was intended, in part, to help bring the two sides closer together.
During his stay in Beirut, Khatibzadeh held what he described as positive talks with senior Lebanese officials, including Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, and representatives of the Foreign Ministry.
Iran calls for an end to hostilities across the region
The Iranian deputy foreign minister stressed that Israel must end its military campaign in Lebanon and across the Levant, arguing that developments on the different regional fronts are closely interconnected.
“One of Iran’s conditions is an end to all wars,” he said, explaining that continued hostilities on any single front would effectively mean the continuation of the broader regional war.
Khatibzadeh said Iran had therefore remained committed to ending the conflict in Lebanon, describing the effort as part of a wider approach to stopping the war throughout the region.
His remarks underscored Tehran’s position that a ceasefire limited to one theater of conflict would not be sufficient to establish lasting regional stability if military operations continued elsewhere.
The Iranian diplomat accused Washington and Tel Aviv of violating the Islamabad understanding through their attacks on Iran and Lebanon. He also said US efforts to secure a ceasefire and end Israel’s war on Lebanon had reached an impasse.
Khatibzadeh questioned Israel’s willingness to honor its commitments, arguing that Washington bore responsibility for restraining its regional ally and ensuring that any agreed arrangements were respected.
Tehran rejects US war aims
Addressing the war against Iran, Khatibzadeh described the US military campaign as illegal under international law and said Washington had failed to eliminate Iran’s air-defense systems and deterrence capabilities.
He said Iran had resisted an existential war and would continue to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
He also reiterated Iran’s readiness to address concerns raised by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the United States regarding its peaceful nuclear activities.
Khatibzadeh pointed to more than 15 IAEA reports that, according to him, confirmed Iran’s compliance with its commitments. He presented this record as evidence that concerns over Iran’s nuclear program could be addressed through engagement rather than military confrontation.
Khatibzadeh also said Iran had proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, signaling Tehran’s readiness to pursue a diplomatic solution to tensions surrounding one of the world’s most strategically important maritime routes.
The Iranian deputy foreign minister stressed that Tehran did not seek war but would resist any conflict imposed on the country.
Hezbollah as a Lebanese political movement
Commenting on Hezbollah, Khatibzadeh described the movement as a Lebanese political party established in response to Israeli attacks and occupation.
He said Iran’s relations with its regional allies were rooted in shared beliefs, values, and principles, presenting these ties as part of Tehran’s broader regional outlook.
The remarks came as Iran continued diplomatic engagement with Lebanon, where the consequences of Israel’s military campaign remain central to regional security discussions.
Khatibzadeh’s statements placed the need for a comprehensive cessation of hostilities at the center of Iran’s approach to ending the conflict, arguing that peace cannot be secured through isolated ceasefires while fighting continues elsewhere.
For Tehran, the central requirement is an end to the war across all fronts, accompanied by respect for national sovereignty and the fulfillment of commitments made through diplomatic agreements.

articles.title: At least 7 killed, dozens injured in explosion during live-fire drill at Canadian military base
articles.body:
At least seven people were killed and dozens more injured Saturday in an explosion and massive fire at a Canadian military base in Alberta, according to military sources cited by Global News, in what officials described as an exceptionally serious disaster that overwhelmed nearby hospitals and sent flames spreading beyond the base's perimeter.
The explosion occurred at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, about 200 kilometers southeast of Edmonton, at approximately 4 p.m. local time. Multiple Canadian Armed Forces sources told Global News that a live-fire training exercise struck a gas pipeline or gas well on the base, triggering the blast. Canadian authorities have not officially confirmed the cause.
The explosion sparked a large fire that spread rapidly amid powerful winds, with gusts reaching 100 kilometers per hour. About three hours after the incident began, local authorities reported that the flames had crossed the base's perimeter fence, prompting firefighters from several jurisdictions to join efforts to contain the blaze.
Ambulances and medical helicopters were dispatched to the base, and casualties were transported to hospitals in Edmonton after medical facilities in the nearby town of Wainwright became overwhelmed by the number of patients requiring treatment.
Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency physician at Edmonton's Royal Alexandra Hospital, told Canadian public broadcaster CBC that the scale of the emergency was extraordinary.
"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Thirsk said. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."
Canadian Defense Minister David McGuinty confirmed that the incident had caused fatalities and injuries but did not provide an official casualty count.
"I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory," McGuinty said Saturday night, describing the situation as "very, very active and delicate."
The minister said authorities had launched an investigation to establish the circumstances of the disaster, with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police involved alongside military personnel and emergency responders.
Prime Minister Mark Carney also addressed the incident in a post on X, calling it a serious emergency.
"Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," he wrote. "We are working closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities."
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it had affected many Canadian military personnel.
By late Saturday night, local authorities reported that firefighters were holding the fire and that property and critical infrastructure were being protected. No evacuation order had been issued for residents of the nearby town.
CFB Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training installations, used to prepare soldiers and military units for operational deployments.
The base houses the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, where military units train to operate together under realistic battlefield conditions, as well as the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides basic infantry and other military training.
The disaster has prompted a large-scale emergency response, with federal, provincial and local authorities working together as investigators seek to determine how a routine military training exercise could have ended in such a deadly incident.

articles.title: Trump eyes reopening Europe to Russian gas – NYT
articles.body:
Trump eyes reopening Europe to Russian gas – NYT
The US plan for securing peace in Ukraine calls for Europe to increase its purchase of Russian gas, while Ukraine would consider reopening pipelines that once carried it to the EU, The New York Times reported on Saturday, citing people familiar with the talks.
The proposal is the latest in a series of steps by US President Donald Trump to broker peace between Moscow and Kiev. It follows an agreement to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports and the waiving of sanctions and tariffs mandated by the late American Senator Lindsey Graham.
Washington has reportedly pitched restoring Russian gas exports to Europe as part of a longer-term plan to offer Moscow economic incentives under a broader settlement. The proposed deal would also address relations between Russia and NATO, security guarantees for Ukraine and territorial issues, the sources told the newspaper.
US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly raised the idea of restoring Russian gas flows to Europe via Ukraine in talks with European and Ukrainian officials, including Vladimir Zelensky during a visit to Kiev in September.
Russian gas exports through neighboring Ukraine were only halted in January 2025, after authorities in Kiev opted not to extend the transit deal with Moscow.
Russia supplied around 45% of the EU’s gas imports before the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022, but sanctions and damage to key infrastructure, such as Nord Stream 1, had cut its share to about 12% by 2025. The bloc nevertheless bought 36 billion cubic meters (bcm) of Russian gas last year, including pipeline supplies and liquefied natural gas (LNG). The latest estimates put the value of EU purchases of Russian LNG at €7.2 billion, nearly €1 billion more than in 2024.
Since the halt of gas transit through Ukraine, TurkStream has been the only remaining route for Russian pipeline gas to the bloc.
Brussels began phasing out gas imports from Russia under some short-term pipeline contracts in June 2026 and plans to ban Russian LNG imports from January 2027 and pipeline gas imports by September, with a complete phaseout targeted by the end of that year.
Meanwhile, Russia has shifted more energy exports to Asia, with deliveries of Russian natural gas to China reaching 38.8 bcm in 2025, up 24.8% from a year earlier. Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Moscow is ready to supply fuel to EU countries but needs a signal from Brussels. He said Russia would assess the feasibility and commercial viability of such exports rather than wait for Europe to “slam the door” on energy ties.

articles.title: Attacked from the sky: Sudanese goldminers count deadly cost of eking out a living on the Egypt border
articles.body:
Torches still fixed on their heads but tools cast aside, the Sudanese goldminers of the North Valley had already mounted an impromptu rescue operation by the time Ammar* arrived at the site of a suspected Egyptian airstrike.
At least 114 were killed, according to the Sudanese rights group Emergency Lawyers, in the strike on Saturday 10 October on an artisanal goldmine brimming with young Sudanese trying to eke out a living in a country where the economy has been shattered by three years of war.
There has been anger in Sudan among those who accuse Egypt of being behind the strike, furious at what they see as aggression by their northern neighbour against workers who produce much of the gold consumed regionally and at the country’s inability to defend itself.
“These are people who have just come here to earn a living, through their own hard work,” says Ammar, a gold trader who worked at a different site and responded to calls to help the survivors.
“Their families are scattered by the war and they send them what they earn,” he says. “Sudan doesn’t have jobs, so they go to the mountains and dig with their hands to live.”
When Ammar arrived, he found chaos at the scene after the strike. The green bags used by the miners to carry excavated materials littered the ground as they abandoned their work to rescue the injured. They made stretchers from blankets, loaded the wounded into pickup trucks to be rushed to nearby towns, and began digging graves for the dead.
The strike was immediately attributed to Egypt by the miners, whose military later confirmed they had carried out operations as part of their push to end “illegal goldmining in the eastern desert”, though they did not address the airstrike.
Egypt reportedly struck the same site in June, killing at least 15 people, according to Sudanese media, and has carried out raids, arresting miners and confiscating equipment.
Egypt said it had distributed leaflets warning civilians to leave before launching the operation. Photos on social media appear to show a leaflet stating: “Surrender yourselves and your equipment. Your lives are more important than any equipment.”
Mohamed Salah, director of Emergency Lawyers, said there were scuffles before the bombing between miners and Egyptian security forces trying to force them out of the area.
“While Egyptian authorities have sought to curb illegal border trade for a long time, locals did not anticipate an escalation involving military aircraft,” says Salah.
He says most of the miners have dispersed since the attack but does not expect them to stay away.
“The miners say they will return – artisanal goldmining in these border areas is the only source of income for them,” he says.
Many come from conflict-hit parts of the country, such as the Darfur and Kordofan regions, he adds, and have slowly made their way through the country’s interior until finding themselves try to make a living prospecting for gold on the Egyptian border.
While Egypt has framed its operations as an attempt to curtail illegal mining, it has been a beneficiary of the informal mining sector, receiving an estimated 60% of the gold produced and smuggled from parts of northern Sudan that border Egypt.
Despite a three-year war between the Sudanese military and rebel paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, gold production has continued in areas controlled by both sides, with artisanal mines proliferating because of rising poverty in the country.
The mines rely on manual labour and expose workers to health risks because of the chemicals used to process the gold, such as mercury and cyanide.
The human rights campaigner Hala al-Karib says the airstrike reveals the vulnerability of the prospectors.
“They are blocked from any other means of livelihood with the collapse of the education system [and] the high rates of unemployment. What other options do they have to survive?” says Karib, who leads the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa network.
“They are at the bottom of the chain because they are subject to the exploitation of big traders. So it is quite painful that on top of that they are exposed to this terror, being killed randomly. It’s a crime and there is nothing to justify it.”
* Name changed to protect his identity

articles.title: Predictions of Gaza’s death toll were wrong - why is no one being held accountable? - opinion
articles.body:
In late September, Gaza’s Hamas-run Health Ministry published its 2025 mortality report, the first since the war began to purport to count every death in Gaza.
Of 24,650 deaths, it attributed 17,286 to “war operations,” without separating combatants from civilians, and 1,584 to accidents. Independent analyst Eirik Schrøder-Bråtane calculated that the remaining 5,780 nonviolent deaths roughly matched Gaza’s prewar annual nonviolent toll. The ministry also recorded 50,227 births.
This was 2025: the year Israel halted aid for 11 weeks after Hamas refused to extend the truce and release more hostages, following a six-week ceasefire during which 25,200 trucks delivered nearly 450,000 tons of aid. Israel said Hamas was seizing and selling supplies to finance its war. By September, Israel counted over two million tons delivered during the war.
It was also the year UN officials warned of babies dying by the thousands and the IPC, the UN-backed hunger monitor, declared famine in Gaza City.
Yet the ministry’s own figures show nothing resembling the mass-mortality footprint those warnings suggested: no surge in nonviolent deaths from hunger, disease, or other indirect causes.
Andrew Fox, a former British Army officer and senior fellow at the Henry Jackson Society, argued in 2024 that Gaza’s war toll was being padded with natural deaths. Now, he wrote, the famine allegations and other claims had been “debunked by Hamas’s own numbers.” The modelers who predicted hundreds of thousands of deaths, he added, “should lose their careers.”
Then he said: “They won’t. They’ll get a free pass.”
That may be the safest prediction anyone has made about this war.
For years, Israel’s accusers have issued confident predictions of mass death and confident counts of massacres. The headlines circle the globe. When the predictions fail, or the numbers collapse, the correction barely travels at all.
On May 20, 2025, the UN’s humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, told BBC Radio 4 that 14,000 babies in Gaza “will die in the next 48 hours” unless aid reached them. Within a day, the UN clarified that the figure meant roughly 14,100 projected cases of severe acute malnutrition among young children under age 5.
Not deaths. Not babies. Not 48 hours.
The report does show deterioration: infant mortality of 15.8 per 1,000 live births and under-five mortality of 33.4, both worse than before the war. But in the year of the UN’s warnings, Gaza’s infant mortality roughly matched Egypt’s peacetime rate of 16.1, and both its rates sat below the global average. Worse, yes. Mass death, no.
In February 2024, researchers at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine and Johns Hopkins projected as many as 85,750 excess deaths in Gaza over six months in a worst-case scenario of escalating war and epidemic disease. Activist outlets ran headlines like “Israel Could Kill 85,000 More Gazans in 6 Months,” and a lead author told US news program Democracy Now! that the escalation scenario was “currently what’s happening in Rafah.” That epidemic never came.
In Sudan’s largely forgotten war, the same London School found the dead going uncounted: some 26,000 violent deaths in Khartoum State alone in the first 14 months, more than monitors had recorded for the entire country, and over 61,000 deaths from all causes.
In Gaza, the alarm far outran the dead. In Sudan, the dead outran the alarm.
In March 2024, the IPC projected famine in northern Gaza by the end of May if fighting and severe aid restrictions continued. By June, its own Famine Review Committee found the evidence did not indicate famine.
The IPC declared famine in the Gaza Governorate in August 2025, over Israel’s objections to its methodology. Somalia’s 2010-2012 famine killed an estimated 258,000 people, including 133,000 children under five. At its peak, it killed about 30,000 people a month.
Incentive to inflate numbers
Gaza’s Health Ministry, an arm of Hamas with every incentive to inflate, reported 455 malnutrition deaths across nearly two years of war, fewer than Somalia’s famine killed in half a day at its height.
By the IPC’s own threshold, two deaths per 10,000 people a day, the declared famine should have killed about 9,000. Hamas’s own ministry counted fewer than 200, across all of Gaza, fewer than the US records in four days.
Rafah followed a familiar pattern. Before Israel entered the city in May 2024, the Palestinian Authority’s Foreign Ministry warned an assault would bring “the annihilation of about 1.5 million Palestinians.” The EU’s then-foreign-policy chief, Josep Borrell, scoffed at evacuating civilians: “Where? To the moon?” Within three weeks, about a million people had evacuated Rafah. There was no annihilation and no apology.
The pattern is older than this war, and it only ever runs in one direction.
In April 2002, during Israel’s operation in Jenin, PA negotiator Saeb Erekat told CNN that Israeli troops had killed more than 500 people. The UN secretary-general’s own report later counted 52 Palestinians dead, at least half of them terrorists, along with 23 Israeli soldiers, and found the 500 figure unsubstantiated. By then, the “Jenin massacre” had entered the world’s vocabulary.
Operation Cast Lead followed the same arc. Hamas initially acknowledged fewer than 50 dead combatants. The since-discredited 2009 Goldstone Report cited a Palestinian Centre for Human Rights tally identifying just 236 of the dead as combatants. Then, in November 2010, Hamas interior minister Fathi Hammad acknowledged that up to 700 men from Hamas’s military wing and security forces had been killed, close to Israel’s count of 709.
Abroad, the dead were nearly all civilians. At home, they were Hamas martyrs.
On October 17, 2023, Hamas’s health authorities instantly blamed Israel for the Ahli hospital explosion and reported nearly 500 dead. American, British, French, and Canadian intelligence assessments concluded that a misfired Palestinian rocket was the likely cause; US intelligence put the toll at a fraction of the ministry’s tally. The New York Times later conceded that its early coverage had relied too heavily on Hamas’s claims.
The progressive Left, which prides itself on following the science, rarely asks why so many catastrophic predictions and claims about Israel fail. A growing faction of the populist Right, the so-called “woke Right,” recycles Hamas figures and UN forecasts it would ridicule on any other subject.
The method works because the claims and predictions do their work before they can be tested. Put Israel in the dock. Push for sanctions or an arms embargo. Pressure Israel, but not those sworn to its destruction. By the time the evidence arrives, the damage is done.
Tom Fletcher still runs the UN’s humanitarian office. The IPC has not retracted its 2025 famine declaration. Newsrooms still headline the forecasts and bury the accounting.
In most fields, predictions this consequential would at least produce an audit. When the subject is Israel, they produce the next failed prediction.
The writer is an attorney, former IDF soldier, and former NYPD officer. He writes widely on Israel, Zionism, antisemitism, and Jewish history. He serves on the board of Herut North America.

articles.title: IRGC spox. lambasts Washington for "Mother of Bombs" threat
articles.body:
In a message on Saturday, Brigadier General Hossein Mohebi said the future belongs to a nation that turns the enemies’ “biggest” threats into a subject of public humor.
Accoridng to the Press TV EN website, the statement comes amid reports that the US military has developed strike plans that could involve using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), also known as the “mother of all bombs,” against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders a resumption of combat operations.
The potential use of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant escalation in the war between Tehran and Washington.
However, officials familiar with military planning discussions say questions remain over whether the weapon would help achieve US strategic objectives.
